messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stands with her hands folded in front of her on the counter, prayer beads wound loosely around one wrist. She doesn't interrupt Vell's finger-tapping, and when he asks if there's anything to ask, she gives the moneylender the kind of steady look she learned in the hospice — the one that says, *tell me what I need to know to walk in safely*.

"The clerk," she says. "What did he die of — and who found him?"

Then she lets her gaze move, unhurried, to the clean desk, and back to Vell's face.

"Has anyone else been sent for the strongbox before us? A landlord with a second key, a relative who came looking, another man in your employ." A pause, not unkind. "If we're walking into a room where a man died three days ago, I'd rather know whether we'll find the door locked, or already open with someone waiting behind it."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell leans an elbow on the counter, but his eyes go to the empty desk first, then back to Vell.

"A few things, since it's our necks on the stairs." He ticks them off on his fingers, the way Vell did. "How did Jassan die? Fever, a fall, or a knife? Because that tells me who else might be in that room before us. Who holds the key now? The cooper, a landlord, the Fist? And who else knows that box is up there? Family, friends, someone he owed money to?"

He pauses, then adds more quietly: "And describe the seal. Wax, whose mark, what colour. If someone's already been at it, I'd rather know it when I see it than have you tell me at your counter tonight that we're the ones who broke it."

Out of game: I'm watching Vell while he answers, especially when he talks about how Jassan died and who else knows. If an Insight roll fits, I'll take it.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Three days dead, and the box is still there. Who’s been keeping watch over it?”

I rest a hand on the counter. “We’ll need the room key and a note for the landlord saying we’re collecting it on your behalf. And tell us what the seal looks like, so we know we’ve got the right box.”

A pause. “How did Ferr die?”

scenes.narration:
Ostrin Vell takes the questions the way he takes coin: one at a time, and slowly.

"His heart," he says to Sefa first. "Wenna Pike found him. She keeps the house over the cooper's yard. She went up for the rent on the morning after and he was in his chair at the table, cold. A man from the Fist came, looked at him and wrote it down. Heart. Jassan was forty-one." His finger stops on the counter. "Hearts stop."

He turns to Pell and Bram together, since they asked the same thing. "Nobody watches it. It is behind Wenna's lock. She has the key, and she has Jassan's rent owing, she tells me. I sent my boy for the box the day before yesterday. She sent him back. Nothing leaves that room, she says, until someone pays what he owed her." His mouth thins. "The box is mine. The rent was his."

While he talks, Pell watches the man's hands and the corners of his eyes, waiting for the place where he goes careful.

"Who else knows?" Vell repeats. "My house. Wenna Pike. Anyone Wenna has talked to in three days, and she talks." A small pause. "He had no family here. His mother was in the Gate, and she has been dead for years."

Pell can't find the seam. Vell stays equally tight from the first word to the last, and his face doesn't show whether that is a dead clerk, a debt owed or something else.

For the seal, Vell opens a drawer under the counter and takes out a brass seal matrix on a short wooden handle. He warms a stub of brown wax at the lamp, lets a drop fall on a scrap of paper and presses the matrix into it. When he lifts it, the mark is a ring with a V inside it and a small flaw at the top of the ring, where the brass once cracked.

"Brown wax. That mark. Jassan sealed for the house. Every box." He pushes the scrap across the counter so it lies between the three of you. "If it is not whole, I will know it."

Then he dips a pen and writes without stopping to think, in a small upright hand: *The bearers collect the strongbox of Jassan Ferr on behalf of the house of Ostrin Vell. Beregost.* He signs it, sands it, shakes it off and lays it on the counter in front of Bram, next to the wax impression.

"The key is Wenna's. I have none." He puts the brass matrix back in its drawer and locks it. "The rent is between her and you, if you choose to pay it. I will not."

Outside, the hammers along the street have found a rhythm. The light in the window has moved a hand's width across the scales. Vell takes the nearest ledger, opens it, and doesn't look at the clerk's desk.

 Pell keeps his eyes on Vell the whole time the moneylender answers. He watches the finger on the counter, the mouth, how long Vell waits before each answer. He doesn't get the read. Every answer comes out at the same clipped pace, with no hitch on Jassan's death and no flicker when he talks about who else knows of the box. Pell leaves the counter knowing no more about what Vell might be holding back than if he had stood there with his eyes shut.

 Pell keeps his eyes on Vell the whole time the moneylender answers. He watches the finger on the counter, the mouth, how long Vell waits before each answer. He doesn't get the read. Every answer comes out at the same clipped pace, with no hitch on Jassan's death and no flicker when he talks about who else knows of the box. Pell leaves the counter knowing no more about what Vell might be holding back than if he had stood there with his eyes shut.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell picks up the wax scrap, turns it to the window light, and runs a thumbnail just short of the crack at the top of the ring, fixing the flaw in his memory. Then he holds it up.

"We'll take this along, if it's all the same to you. Easier to match a mark side by side than from memory in a dim room." He tucks it into an inner pocket without waiting long for an answer.

"How much does Wenna say he owed? And your boy, what's his name, and did he get past her door, or did she stop him on the stairs?" A beat. "If someone's been in that room since, I'd like to know whether it was before or after she turned him away."

His eyes drift once more to the tidy, empty desk, then back to Vell's bent head. "Did Jassan carry anything of the house's on him? A key to the box, papers, a ring? The Fist man who wrote 'heart' — did he take anything away?"

Whatever Vell answers, Pell straightens off the counter and nods toward the door to the other two. "Coast Way, then. Let's see the cooper's yard before the day gets on."

Out of game: unless something Vell says changes things, Pell is ready to head straight to Wenna Pike's.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I leave the letter on the counter for now.

“You sent a boy, and she refused him. Now you’re paying three armed strangers to try again. How much rent is owing?”

My voice stays level. “I won’t draw steel on a landlady over her tenant’s debts. If we settle with her, will you deduct what we pay from Ferr’s estate and reimburse us—with a receipt, up to a sum we agree now? Otherwise our fee’s not seventy-five gold. It’s whatever’s left.”

scenes.narration:
Vell watches Pell lift the wax scrap off the counter and turn it to the window. He doesn't reach for it.

"Keep it. It is wax." He goes back to his ledger, and then, since the questions keep coming, closes it on one finger to hold the page.

"Three gold and some silver. That is what she told the boy." He gives the next answers in order, tapping the closed ledger once for each. "The boy is Mott. He did not get past her door. She met him on the stairs with her arms folded, he says, and he came down again." A short pause. "If anyone has been in since, Wenna will know. It is her house."

The question about what Jassan had on him takes a moment longer. "He kept the box key on a cord round his neck. The Song of the Morning took him for burial. Whether the key went with him, ask them." His eyes don't move toward the empty desk. "The Fist man I never saw. He came to the house, not here. He wrote it in their book at the garrison. Whatever he took, he did not bring to me."

Bram's question gets a longer look than any of the others. Vell sits with the ledger shut on his finger, working the sum out before he answers.

"I will not pay Wenna Pike." He says it as plainly as before. "But I owe Jassan his wages for the last tenday. Four gold. He has no heirs here to claim it." He sets the ledger down. "Bring me her receipt for the rent, signed, with the box. I will pay it to you out of his wages, on top of the seventy-five. Up to four gold. Not a copper over, and no receipt, no money." He takes up his pen again. "That is his debt settled from his own pay. It is not mine."

The bearer's note still lies on the counter beside the empty space where the wax scrap was. Sefa is still standing at the counter. Pell has straightened up and is looking at the door. Outside, a cart rattles past toward the Coast Way, and one of the smithies starts a new piece with three heavy strokes. Vell goes back to writing figures in his small, upright hand.

 (Out of game: none of these four needed a roll. Each one is ordinary handling, a question, or a character's own words, and each succeeds as declared.)

Pell slips the wax scrap into the inner pocket of his jerkin. The bearer's note stays on the counter where Bram left it.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Put that beneath the letter and sign it. Up to four gold against Wenna’s receipt, in addition to our fee.”

Once he’s done, I take the letter and head out with the others toward the cooper’s yard.

“Let’s speak to Wenna before we spend anything,” I say to Sefa and Pell. “She found Ferr. Might be she can tell us more than ‘hearts stop.’”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa picks up the bearer's note, folds it once along its crease and holds it out toward Bram.

"Here — you asked for this. One of us should carry it, and you'll likely make a straighter impression on a landlady than a man with a book of prayers at his belt." A half-smile. "I'll keep the soft word in reserve, if she has her arms folded."

She turns back to Vell only long enough to nod, once. "Before nightfall, then."

As she moves toward the door, she says to the others, more quietly: "Three gold and a handful of silver is cheaper than starting the morning with a fight in a stairwell. Let's see what Wenna Pike actually wants before we open our purses."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell picks the bearer's note up off the counter, blows the last grains of sand from it, folds it once and holds it out to Bram.

"Your idea, your paper. You've the face for landladies." Something close to a grin. "Four gold on a receipt's a fair deal. Wenna gets her rent, nobody draws steel, and we get paid twice for it."

He gives Vell a short nod, the kind you give a man you'll see again tonight. "Before nightfall, seal whole. You'll have it."

At the door he waits for the other two, then speaks low as they step into the noise of the street.

"Two things I don't like. The key on his neck, and a Fist man nobody's seen. Somebody may have had that box open and closed again, and I want to be the one who notices, not Vell." He settles his satchel strap. "Wenna first. I'll pay her the three and silver out of my own purse if we have to; we get it back on the receipt. While you two talk to her, I'll look at the stairs, the door and the lock before anyone walks in and muddies things. If the box key's not in that room, the Song of the Morning's our next stop."

He sets off toward the Coast Way at an easy walk, eyes already on the rooflines and the gaps between houses, the way they always are.

Out of game: Pell heads straight to the cooper's yard. When we arrive I'd like to see the house from the street first: windows, back stairs, whether the room above can be reached any way besides Wenna's door.

scenes.narration:
Vell doesn't argue. He has already worked the sum once, and he doesn't do it twice. He pulls the bearer's note back across the counter, dips the pen and writes beneath his signature in the same small upright hand, without stopping: *Up to four gold of J. Ferr's owed wages, against W. Pike's signed receipt for his rent, paid with the fee on delivery of the box, seal whole.* He signs it a second time, sands the fresh line and pushes the paper back.

Two hands go for it at once. Pell gets it off the counter first and blows the sand from the new ink. Sefa has her fingers on the other corner, so the note gets folded once along its crease between the two of them and ends up in Bram's hand.

"Before nightfall," Vell says to Sefa's nod. He answers Pell's with a nod of his own, short and level, and he has opened the ledger again before the door shuts behind them.

---

Out on the street the noise is louder. Beregost runs on charcoal and iron. Smoke hangs low over the roofs, and the hammering comes from three directions, never quite together. Pell talks quietly as they walk. The Coast Way runs west off the high street past a farrier's, a chandler's and two houses with washing out, and it's a short walk, a quarter of an hour at an easy pace with carts making them step aside twice.

The cooper's yard is easy to find, because you hear it before you see it. Someone is driving hoops onto a barrel with a mallet, slow and steady, and stops every few strokes to check the fit.

The house sits over the yard and comes right up to the street. It's two storeys of timber on a stone footing, with a plastered front gone yellow. The ground-floor window stands open, with a curtain and a pot of something green on the sill. A woman's voice inside is telling someone off for the state of the step. Upstairs, the two front windows have their shutters open.

Pell looks the house over from the far side of the lane while the other two head for the gate. Reading a house is his trade, and it doesn't take him long. Through the open street door he can see a narrow inner stair, and that's the only way up from inside. It passes the landlady's door at the bottom. The yard runs back along the side of the house behind a gate of grey planks. Through the gaps there are stacked staves, a row of finished barrels and a lean-to roof of old shingles built against the back wall. It stands about eight feet high. Above it is a single upstairs window with its shutters closed and a bar or a hasp holding them shut from inside, judging by how flat they sit. That window faces the yard rather than the street, and it's the only upstairs window on the house that's shut. A man who climbs well could get onto the lean-to from the barrels and reach the sill with his hands. Doing it in daylight, in front of whoever is working that mallet, is another matter.

Then Pell sees the gatepost, and that's what keeps him looking.

On the left post of the yard gate, at about knee height where nobody walking by looks, someone has drawn a small chalk mark: a circle with a short stroke down through it, and beside it a tick angled up toward the house. To anyone else it's a child's scribble. Pell learned it on the roofs above the Wide before he could spell his own name. In the cant of the Gate it means *eyes on this. Spoken for. Keep off.* The chalk is clean and bright. No rain has run it and no boot has scuffed it. It went up in the last day or two.

Beregost has smiths, a temple and a Fist garrison. It has no Guild. That mark belongs to a city three days up the road.

Behind the gate the mallet stops. A broad, bald man in a leather apron puts his head round the end of the barrel row, sees a man in chain mail with a shield and a paper in his hand at the gate, and doesn't come any closer. He calls over his shoulder toward the house, not loudly: "Wenna. More of them."

The voice from the ground-floor window stops in the middle of what it was saying.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stays a half-step behind Bram and to one side, where the mallet-man can see both her hands. She doesn't reach for the gate.

"Mistress Pike?" she calls toward the house, mildly, over the quiet left by the stopped mallet. "We've come about Jassan Ferr's room. We'd rather speak to you first than go tramping up your stair like the last one. And we'll mind the step."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell crosses the lane at the same easy pace and stops beside the gatepost. He crouches as if a bootlace has come loose, takes a closer look at the chalk without touching it, and straightens again.

He steps up behind Bram and Sefa and speaks low, without moving his lips much:

"Don't look down. Left gatepost, knee height. Guild chalk from the Gate, a day or two old. It means *spoken for, someone's watching, keep off.* Beregost has no Guild, so somebody brought it with them." He tips his head a fraction toward the house. "And you heard him. *More of them.* We're not the first today."

Then, louder and friendly, to the bald man in the apron, with a nod at the barrels: "Good hoops. Who were the others, master cooper? We'd hate to be tripping over Vell's other errand-boys on the stairs."

While the cooper answers and Wenna comes to her door, Pell lets Bram and his paper take the front. He drifts half a step aside, where he can see the lane both ways, the windows across the street and the mouths of the alleys. The chalk means eyes, and he wants to know whose. He also notes who is in the yard besides the cooper, and whether the closed shutters upstairs have been forced or scratched from outside.

He leaves the mark exactly as it is. Rubbing it out would tell whoever drew it that someone here reads cant.

Out of game: I'd like a Perception roll for spotting anyone watching the house, and I'm listening closely to what the cooper and Wenna say about the earlier visitors: how many, when, what they looked like, and whether they went upstairs.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I read the letter twice, fold it carefully and tuck it inside my coat. For a moment I stand still, jaw tight. Then I turn back to the gate, keeping Vell’s paper lowered.

“Morning. Bram Halloway. We’ve come to speak with Mistress Pike about Jassan Ferr’s strongbox—and settle his rent against a signed receipt. No need for trouble.”

I wait outside rather than letting myself in. “Vell’s boy should have come prepared to pay. We understand he didn’t.”

scenes.narration:
The ground-floor curtain twitches. Then the street door opens and a woman comes out onto the step. She's short and broad in the hip, somewhere past fifty, with her sleeves pushed up and a rag in one fist. A ring of three keys hangs from a cord at her apron. She looks at the step first, as if checking that nobody has dirtied it since she last told someone off about it, and then she looks at the three of them.

"Well, somebody was raised right," she says to Sefa. "*Mind the step.* That boy of Vell's came up it like a goat. Tobin, it's all right, they're not the other one." The cooper doesn't go back to his mallet just yet.

Before he turns back to the gate, Bram puts a folded paper away inside his coat and stands still for a moment with his jaw set. Vell's note stays low in his other hand. Wenna watches him do it, then hears him out, and her arms come up and fold across her chest. She doesn't look like she's refusing anyone. She looks like she's settling in for a long talk.

"Prepared to pay. Well. *Somebody's* listening at last." She points the rag up the stair. "Three gold and four silver, that's what Jassan owed me. Five weeks, and the last two I let slide because he was a quiet man and paid regular before. I said three and *some* to the boy because I'm not going to stand on my own step reckoning silver at a child. Three and four. You want a receipt, I'll write you one. I can write my name, thank you, and the sum, and the day." She sniffs. "And nothing goes down those stairs till it's in my hand. I told the boy that and I'll tell Vell to his face if he ever walks this far."

Pell crouches by the gatepost for a moment over his bootlace, then gets up and leans in close to the others. When he asks the cooper about the hoops and the others, the bald man gives the barrels a look as if they might answer for him. He rubs his scalp with the back of a hand.

"Boy, day before yesterday. Vell's." His voice is slow, the same pace as his mallet. "Then a fellow last evening, near lamplight. Not Vell's, he said so himself. Lean, taller than you. Brown coat, good boots, city voice." He looks at Pell a beat longer than at the others. "Like yours, a bit. Gate. He stood about the yard a while before he knocked. Didn't go up. She'd not have him."

"I'd not have him *yet*," Wenna corrects him. "Very civil, he was, I'll say that. Offered to pay Jassan's rent, all of it, there and then, and carry the box off and save me the bother. messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell steps back in beside Bram, already working the purse loose from his belt.

"Then let's not make you wait on anyone's turn, mistress." He counts it out on his palm where she can see every coin: three gold, four silver, and lays it on the flat of her rag-free hand. "Three and four, as you said. Write the receipt for Jassan Ferr's rent, paid in full, today's date, and your name under it. Bram'll hold it; he's the tidy one."

While she weighs the coins, he keeps his voice easy, as if passing the time.

"That civil fellow from last night. Did he give a name? Or say when today he'd be back, morning or lamplight again?" A small shrug. "Only so we're gone before he comes and you've no awkward words on your step."

Then, more carefully: "When you found Jassan in his chair, was there a cord round his neck? A key on it? And the Fist man who came after, did he touch anything in the room, open anything, take anything down the stairs with him?"

Once the receipt is written and the key is off the ring, Pell holds out a hand for it. "I'll go up first, if you don't mind. Light feet. I'd like to see that door and lock before three of us tramp through." He glances at Bram and Sefa. "Give me a minute on the landing before you follow. Keep Mistress Pike company."

On the stair he moves quietly, watching the treads for fresh mud or scuffs, and stops at the door before putting the key in. He checks the keyhole and the plate for fresh scratches, the frame for marks of a pry, and the gap underneath for light or movement.

Out of game: Pell pays Wenna 3 gp 4 sp from his own purse (that leaves him 28 gp, 2 sp). I'd like an Investigation roll on the door and lock, then a look at the room from the threshold before anyone goes in: the chair, the table, the box, and anything moved or out of place.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Three gold and four silver. Fair enough.” I show Wenna the signed authority. “Pell, you offered to cover it. Still willing?”

I glance along the lane, then back to her. “That fellow give a name, or say how he knew Jassan?”

I lower my voice a little. “And before we go up—was anything disturbed when you found him? Anything you thought odd? We’ve only had Vell’s account. You were there.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa doesn't reach for the keys or the gate. She leaves her hands to rest one over the other and looks at Wenna, not at the ring in her fist.

"Then you did Vell a kindness you didn't have to, and nobody's thanked you for it." Her voice is warm, plain. "This other one — did he give you a name? Did he ask to see the box, or just carry it off? And when you told him to wait his turn, did he stay about the lane?"

She lets the question sit for a beat, then says, quieter, as if she's sharing something rather than pressing: "If he said he'd come back, it's because he means to. We'd rather settle the rent now, take your receipt, and have that box gone from your house before he hears Vell's people have already come and gone."

She glances at Pell and Bram. "Three and four is fair, and you'll have it in your hand before we step off the street."

screens.Pell Dunmore:
Bram asked Wenna to confirm the three gold and four silver, showed her the signed authority, and asked whether Pell was still willing to pay. Sefa stayed away from the keys and the gate. She thanked Wenna warmly for the kindness she did Vell, and said the group wanted to settle the rent and take the box away before the other man returned. Both of them asked whether he had given a name, and Bram also asked whether anything had been disturbed when Jassan was found.

Wenna takes the coins off your palm one at a time. She turns each gold piece over and bites the third. The four silver go into her apron pocket unlooked at.

"Three and four. There. That's the first honest money anyone's brought up this step in three days." Her face loosens, and she says it to Sefa more than to the men. "No, nobody's thanked me. Vell least of all. I'd half given up on hearing it."

She fetches a pencil stub and a torn almanac flyleaf and writes against the doorframe, slowly, pressing hard, with the sum in figures and in words. *Recd of the bearers for the house of Vell, rent owed by Jassan Ferr, five weeks, three gold four silver, paid in full.* She adds the day and *Wenna Pike*, with a practised flourish on the P. Bram holds out Vell's note. She reads it, lips moving, and lays her receipt on top of it in his hand.

"The tidy one, is it. Well, you've a tidy face for it."

Then she answers all of you at once.

"He gave a name. Brannock. Said it like I ought to have heard it, which I hadn't. Said he spoke for a Master Thale, who lends money up and down the Way, and that it was a *private* matter, which in my experience means it's anything but. How he knew Jassan he didn't say, and I didn't ask. He never asked to *see* the box. Asked was it sealed, and was the seal whole, and had anybody been at it. Twice he asked that." She jerks her chin up the lane toward the high street. "Then he walked off that way, easy as you like. Said he'd come back today before midday, when he'd seen to his business."

Tobin speaks from behind the barrels without coming closer. "Stood by the gate a good while first. Crouched down once. I thought he'd dropped something."

You keep your eyes off the gatepost.

As for Jassan, Wenna's mouth goes thin, and for the first time she isn't in a hurry.

"In his chair, at the table, head back like he'd nodded off over his sums. Lamp burnt dry. There was a cord round his neck, yes, and something small on it under his shirt. I didn't touch it. I don't rob the dead, whatever Vell's boy thinks. The brothers from the Song came for him that afternoon and took him as he was, cord and all." She turns the key ring in her fingers. "The Fist man felt his wrist, looked in his face, wrote in his little book and went. Touched nothing else, took nothing down my stair. Odd?" She thinks about it honestly. "There was a smell. Bitter, like the herb-woman's shop. And he'd had a fire in the grate, and it's not been cold enough nights for a fire. That's all. I opened the front shutters to air it, and I've not been up since."

She works one plain iron key with a worn bow off the ring and puts it in your outstretched hand. She doesn't let go straight away. "I'll want that back. I'll be at the foot of the stair."

---

The stair is narrow and steep and smells of old timber and lye. You take it on the edges of the treads, where they don't creak. The dust tells the story Wenna told. There are big careless scuffs on the lower steps that stop halfway up, which is the boy turned back. Above that there are only the small blunt prints of a woman's shoe, going up and coming down, and older marks under the dust where a man carried something heavy feet-first down the stair. Nothing is fresher than that.

The door at the top is plain pine with a box lock screwed to the inside and a brass escutcheon on the outside. The brass around the keyhole has the dull, even wear of one key used for years. There are no bright scratches from a pick and no shine on the wards where something else was tried. The frame is unmarked by any bar or blade, and the paint hasn't cracked at the strike plate. Daylight comes under the door from the open front shutters, steady, with no shadow moving across it. Nobody has worked this lock but its own key.

The key turns with a heavy click. You push the door open a hand's width, then all the way, and stay on the threshold.

It's a single room under the slope of the roof. Morning comes in through the two front windows, and the back window over the yard is shuttered and barred from inside with a wooden peg through the hasp, just as it looked from the lane. There's a narrow bed, made, with a blanket folded square at its foot. A washstand. A row of pegs by the door holds a hat and a scarf and nothing else, and there's an empty space between them where something heavier once hung and stretched the wood. A table under the front windows, with the chair pushed back from it at an angle, the way a chair sits after the man in it has been lifted out. A tin lamp on the table, its glass black with soot. Below him, at the foot of the stair, Wenna stands with her arms folded and her eyes on the stair, and doesn't come up. Bram and Sefa are with her in the doorway, with the yard and the lane behind them. In the yard Tobin has picked up his mallet again. After a moment the slow knock of the hoops starts up, one stroke and then another.

The rules:
- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.
- Add nothing beyond your narration and the players' messages. Never reveal what only the game master knows.
- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.
- Write the screens in the order you are asked for them.

Then say who is where at the end of it: group the characters who are together (can see and hear each other) — every character in this scene in exactly one group; a character from elsewhere who, by your narration, is now with them joins their group — and name each one's place in a few words.
Then say who is waiting at the end of it: a character in this scene who is asleep, unconscious, or has said they wait for something named (until dawn, until another comes back) and has nothing to decide until it comes — with what ends the wait, in a few words. A character with anything to decide is never waiting.

scenes.narration:
Bram moves to the wall side of the stair foot. That leaves the treads clear and puts his shoulder where he can see the gate and a slice of the lane through the street door. Sefa stays by the newel post. Between the two of them, Wenna ends up standing on her own step with her key ring, being asked things, and she seems happy enough about it.

She answers Bram first, because his was the simpler question.

"Visitors? Up my stair? No. Not in five weeks, not one, I'd have heard them. That stair talks." She tips her head back at it. "He wasn't a man for callers. He'd go out to Vell's in the morning, back at dusk, and the lamp would be going up there till all hours. That last tenday more than ever. I'd see it under his door when I locked up." She stops, and turns the rag over in her hand. "Frightened. Well. I'll be honest with you, I didn't think it at the time. messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't step in yet. He leans back over the stairwell and calls down, quiet but clear.

"Bram, Sefa, come up. Walk on the edges of the treads, and stop at the door." To Wenna, warmer: "Nothing's leaving, mistress. Just looking."

When they're on the landing, he speaks low, for them only.

"Three things. The box seal's green, not brown, and there's something grey under the wax. Vell said brown, his V, every box. So either Jassan sealed this one with someone else's wax, or someone's been at it. Nobody touches the box." He nods at the stool. "Sefa, there's a vial by the bed and a spill on the floor that smells bitter. You knew a hospice. Tell me if that's medicine or something worse. Don't uncork it."

Then he goes in, keeping to the wall, where the dust and old prints are.

**The box first.** He crouches at eye level with the table's corner, takes the wax scrap from his pocket and holds it beside the seal without letting them touch. He looks for the ring, the V, the crack at the top, and for whatever the grey metal under the wax is: a lead disc, a second seal, a plug in the keyhole. He checks whether the wax is whole or has been lifted and pressed back, and whether the padlock or hasp shows any fresh brightness.

**The grate next.** He kneels and uses a dagger point to ease the unburnt curl of paper out of the ash, careful not to crumble it, and tilts it to the window to read what's left of the ink.

**Last, the clean floorboard.** He runs a fingertip along the seam, then slides the dagger tip in at the end and lifts it gently, ready to stop if it sticks or anything is rigged underneath.

To Bram, without looking up: "Keep an eye on the lane from the front window. Brannock said before midday. I'd like to know if he's early."

Out of game: I'd like an Investigation roll comparing the seal to Vell's impression and reading the burnt paper, and I'll check under the board before reaching into anything. Money looks right to me: 28 gp, 2 sp, plus the electrum and copper.

scenes.narration:
Pell leans out over the stairwell and calls down, quietly. His voice carries down the narrow stair to the street door. Then he turns back into the room and keeps to the wall, where the dust has old prints in it already.

He goes to the box first. He crouches until his eyes are level with the corner of the table, takes the brown wax scrap from his jerkin and holds it an inch from the green seal without letting the two touch.

There is no ring on it, no V and no crack. Vell's brown drop looks small next to it. This seal was never his. A disc of grey lead, about the width of a thumb joint, lies flat across the join of the lid, and green wax has been poured over it and around its edges so that the lid can't lift without breaking the lead or the wax. Something pressed the lead hard enough that the mark shows through the thin skin of wax on top: a pair of scales, the pans level, and above them an eye drawn as one closed curve with lashes, like a sleeper's.

Pell gives it the slow look he would give any seal he was paid to lift and put back. Nobody has done that to this one. The wax runs into the grain of the oak in one unbroken pour, and the edge has no hairline where a hot blade went under it. A fine grey film of dust lies evenly over the top, with no fingerprints in it. The padlock and the hasp are dull iron, and the keyhole shows no bright scratches. Whoever sealed this box, nobody has opened it since.

When he tilts his head to catch the window light along the wax, he sees something else. Deep in the green, under the surface, runs a faint grain of fine curving lines packed close, like the whorls of a thumb. They are too even for a thumb, though. Every line is the same distance from the next, and they circle the stamp the way ripples circle a dropped stone. He has seen a lot of wax in his time, and wax doesn't set like that by itself.

Next he goes to the grate. He kneels on the boards, works the point of a dagger under the browned curl at the back and lifts it out of the ash a finger's width at a time, steadying it against the flat of the blade. It comes out whole. When he turns it to the window the ink is a man's careful, upright hand, smaller than Vell's, and most of the bottom half has burnt to black lace. The top line is clear:

*To Sergeant Cowl of the Fist, at the garrison —*

Below that, between a scorched hole and a run of words too charred to read, one line survives:

*— the notes were sold before the wagons —*

The rest is gone into the fire.

Last is the board by the bed. Pell runs a fingertip along the clean seam. It's smooth, and the edges of the wood are worn round from being handled. messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa listens, and when Tobin mentions the long knife, she lets a small quiet settle before she answers. She isn't shocked; she nods as if fitting a piece.

"Then he wasn't a clerk on an errand. A man who carries a purse he's proud of and a blade he's used to, and asks twice whether the seal's whole." She looks at Wenna. "You were right to keep him off your stair. If he's back before we're gone, don't put yourself between him and the room, whatever he offers. Just keep him talking at the step. Tobin'll be close, and so will we."

She turns her head a little toward the yard. "You said the back shutter was barred more than usual. Is it still barred now — from the inside?"

Then, almost idly, as if remembering: "The Jovial Juggler. That's his master's name. We'll know where to carry a question if this Brannock comes asking after a box we've already taken."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“I’m not saying murder, Mistress Pike. You’ve told us what you saw. That’s all I’m asking.”

I glance up the stair and listen for Pell before turning back to her.

“If Brannock comes while we’re upstairs, you needn’t argue with him. The rent’s paid and Vell’s collectors are here. Just call us down.”

I keep watch on the lane while Pell has his minute.

scenes.narration:
Wenna hears Bram out. Her shoulders come down a little.

"Well. No. You didn't say it." She turns the key ring over once. "I'll call. I've a voice for it, ask Tobin. They hear me at the farrier's."

"They do," Tobin says.

Sefa's warning gets a longer look, and Wenna doesn't take it as well as Bram's. "My own step, in my own house, and I'm not to stand between a man and my own stair." She sniffs. "I'll keep him talking. That I can do with my eyes shut." Then, because Sefa asked about the shutter: "Barred, yes. From inside, a peg through the hasp. He did that himself, his last tenday, and I've not touched it. I opened the *front* ones to air the room, not that one." Sefa calls the Jovial Juggler Brannock's master, and she corrects it at once. "The *Juggler*'s an inn, love, on the high street, with a painted man throwing balls on the sign. Thale's the master. Wherever *he* is."

Tobin has come as far as the gatepost and stops there, with his mallet hanging from one hand. "I'll be about. In the yard," he says to Sefa, and nobody could call it a promise.

Bram looks up the stair and listens. Pell's call came down a moment ago, quiet and clear: *come up, keep to the edges of the treads, stop at the door*. Since then there's only the small creak of a board under someone careful.

Then there are quick bare feet on the lane, and a girl of nine or ten ducks in at the street door. She's skinny and brown from the sun and out of breath, with a copper clenched in her fist like she's been paid and means to keep it. She looks at Sefa and then at Wenna, and settles on the man in chain mail with the shield, as if she was told what to look for.

"You Bram Halloway?" She doesn't wait for him to say so. She has a message by heart and wants to be shot of it, and she rattles it off loud enough for the whole stairwell. "Mistress Brand says, did you get her letter, the one about Vell's box. She says it's got to be before the box goes back, you know what. She's at the Song of the Morning, by the east door, till midday. That's all." She draws breath. "She said you'd know her. She's in grey."

Then she's gone, back up the Coast Way at a run, before anyone can ask her a thing.

Wenna's eyebrows have gone up. She looks at Bram, and at the coat where the folded paper went, and for once she doesn't say anything. In the yard Tobin puts the mallet down on a barrel head without striking it. Across the lane the rug-woman's window is shut, and down the Coast Way the dog barks again, once.

messages.text:
Pell lifts the oilcloth bundle out of the hollow on the flat of his palm and weighs it a moment without untying it. Then he sets the board back in place, sitting it exactly as it was, and carries the bundle to the table, away from the box.

He keeps his voice low, for Bram and Sefa on the landing:

scenes.narration:
Pell lifts the bundle out of the hollow on the flat of his palm. It's heavier than its size, the way metal is, and it feels cool through the oilcloth. He seats the board back in its place, edge to edge, and the clean seam settles in line with the dusty ones on either side. Then he carries the bundle to the table and sets it down at the near end, an arm's length from the box.

He speaks low toward the door, and the landing is empty. Nobody has come up the stair. From below, under the knock of Tobin's mallet, come voices. One is high and quick, a child's, rattling something off, and the words are lost in the stairwell before they reach the top. Then a pause, and quick bare feet going away.

He slips the burnt paper flat inside the cover of his tool roll, where it can't crumble, and starts on the knots.

They're plain hitches pulled tight, and they come loose for a patient thumbnail. He lays the string out straight on the table in the order it came off, so it can go back the same way. The oilcloth folds back in three flaps.

Inside are two things.

The first is a seal matrix, stubby, about as long as his middle finger. The handle is dark wood worn smooth by a hand, waisted in the middle for the grip. It's capped with a squat collar of dull grey metal that is too hard for lead and too dark for pewter. The face is cut in reverse, the way a matrix should be, and when he tips it to the window it's the box's mark exactly. A pair of scales with the pans level. Above them an eye drawn as one closed curve with lashes, like a sleeper's. The line of the beam, the length of the lashes and the slight lean of the left-hand pan all match what's pressed into the lead under the green wax. Vell's brown V on its scrap of paper has nothing in common with it. They come from different hands and different houses.

The second thing is a stub of wax, the same deep bottle green, about the length of his thumb, with one end melted round from use.

There is no key. The bundle holds nothing for the padlock.

Two more things catch his eye on the matrix. Round the rim of the face, outside the scales and the eye, runs a ring of hair-fine engraved lines, close-set and even, circling the mark the way ripples circle a dropped stone. That is the same grain he saw deep in the wax. Somebody cut it into the metal on purpose. And on one side of the grey collar there is a notch. It's small and square-cut, the width of a knife's back, with a matching tooth standing proud just beside it, as if the collar was made to lock against something shaped the same way. A notch like that does nothing on its own.

Up the side of the wooden handle, small and worn nearly flat, runs a line of cut letters. They aren't Common, and they aren't any cant he knows. In the window light they're a row of hooks and short strokes that his eye slides off.

Down in the yard Tobin's mallet keeps its slow pace.

 (Out of game: actions 1–3 needed no roll. They're careful handling in Pell's own trade with nothing pushing back, and the narration plays each one out: the board set back, the knots worked loose and the string laid out in order, the matrix compared against the box seal and Vell's V.)

(Out of game: action 4 is said aloud, but Bram is downstairs at the stair foot in his own scene and doesn't hear it. That's why the narration has Pell speak to an empty landing, and why nobody is at the front window.)

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I let out a slow breath, then turn to Sefa.

“I got a letter on the way here. Harl died owing Vell forty gold. Odda Brand says the note’s in this box, and once it goes back, Vell means to call the debt against her house. She’s asking me to buy the note before then.”

I tap my coat over the letter. “I’ve twenty-seven gold with the silver and copper counted. Not enough. I meant to speak once we’d dealt with the room.”

At Pell’s call, I go up carefully along the edges of the treads and stop at the doorway as he asked.

“What have you found?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa doesn't chase the girl. She turns her head just enough to watch her go, then looks back at Bram, her voice low but clear enough for him.

"She knew your name and where to find you, before we've even carried the box down. That isn't chance — that's somebody with ears in the street." A pause. "Still, it can wait the half hour it takes to finish what we were hired for. Let's get the box out of this house first. Then decide whether this Brand's message is a letter or a lure."

She glances up the stair, then to Wenna. "Do you know a Mistress Brand — grey-haired, east door of the Song? Does Jassan's name ever sit with hers?"

scenes.narration:
Bram doesn't lower his voice much, and it's a narrow stairwell. Wenna is three steps from him with her key ring, and Tobin stands at the gatepost. Both of them hear it all: Harl, forty gold, Vell's note in the box, a house called on the debt.

(Out of game: by my records Bram has twenty-three gold, fourteen silver and thirty copper, a little under twenty-five gold counted together, not twenty-seven. Tell me if I've got that wrong.)

Sefa lets the girl's bare feet fade up the Coast Way before she answers, low and level, just for Bram. The other two hear her anyway.

Bram doesn't wait for the rest. He takes the stair the way Pell told them to, on the edges of the treads, and the old wood barely creaks under the chain mail.

Below him, Wenna answers Sefa, and the stairwell carries every word of it up after him.

"In *grey*, love. The child said in grey. Odda Brand's not grey-haired, she's younger than you'd think." She turns the key ring over once, and this time she's slower to start. "I know her to nod to. Everyone on this side of town does. Harl Brand was her man. He drove wagons south for whoever was hiring, a carter, a good one. He went down the Way to Nashkel with a train at the turn of last month and none of them came back. Not the wagons, not the drivers, not a mule." She looks at Bram's back going up the stair, and then at Sefa. "Jassan never said her name to me. He never said anybody's name. But forty gold on Harl's house..." Her mouth goes thin. "That's Vell. He'd call a note on a widow's roof with the man three weeks gone and think himself honest for it."

"Hauled my barrels," Tobin says from the gatepost. "To Nashkel. Twice a year." He stops there. That's as far as he knows it.

Bram reaches the landing. The door of Jassan's room stands open, and morning light from the front windows lies across the boards and the threshold. From the doorway the iron-bound box is plain on the far corner of the table, and so is the deep green of its seal. He stops on the threshold as he was asked and puts his question into the room.

In the yard below, Tobin's mallet stays where he left it on the barrel head. Wenna stands at the foot of the stair with her arms folded. She's looking up the stair, not at her step.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell glances at the empty landing, then back at the table. He works fast and tidily. The matrix and the green stub go back into the oilcloth, the three flaps folded as they were, and the string is retied in the same hitches, in the order it came off. The bundle goes into the inner pocket of his jerkin, opposite the wax scrap.

*Not Vell's mark. Not Vell's business. Not leaving it under a board for Brannock either.*

He steps to the front window and stands to one side of the frame, not in it. He looks down at the lane: the step, the gate, the alley mouths, and which way a pair of quick bare feet might have run. He looks for a small figure going toward the high street, and for anyone waiting at the corner for it.

On his way back past the bed he crouches by the stool. He wraps the dark vial in the scarf from the peg without uncorking it and slides it into his satchel among the potions, wedged so it can't knock against them.

He leaves the box where it is. He doesn't touch it, and the dust on it stays as it was.

At the head of the stair he leans over and calls down, quiet and even:

"Bram? Sefa? Who was the little one, and what did they want?" A beat. "Come up when you can, both of you. Edges of the treads. There's something here I want Sefa's eyes on before anyone lifts that box."

Out of game: Pell keeps the bundle and the vial. Before he moves the box, he wants Sefa to look at the rippled wax and the vial, and he wants to know what the child said downstairs. If Brannock's in the lane, I want to see him before he sees me at the window.

scenes.narration:
Pell works quickly and doesn't hurry. The matrix goes back onto the oilcloth face down, with the green stub beside it, and he folds the three flaps back in the order they came open. The waxed string goes on in the same plain hitches, the first one first, each pulled to the same tightness. The bundle sits as it did under the board, only now it's in his hand. It goes into the inner pocket of his jerkin, on the opposite side from Vell's brown scrap. Through the leather it's a cold weight against his ribs.

He takes the front window from the side and keeps his shoulder to the wall. The open shutter covers half his face.

Below him the Coast Way is quiet. The rug-woman's window across the lane is shut. A handcart of charcoal stands by the farrier's with nobody at its shafts. Both alley mouths are empty and shadowed, and nothing in them moves. Up the lane toward the high street, a long way off, a small bare-legged figure goes round the corner by the chandler's at a run without looking back. Then she's gone. Nobody steps out after her, and nobody at that corner turns to watch her pass. Straight below, Tobin stands at the gatepost with his mallet hanging from one hand. His bald head is tipped toward the street door, and he's listening to something inside the house. There's no brown coat anywhere in the lane, and no tall lean man taking his time. If Brannock is coming before midday, he isn't here yet.

On his way back Pell crouches by the stool. The vial stays stoppered. He doesn't put his nose to it, and the bitter smell still hangs over the dried ring on the boards. He lifts the scarf off its peg. It's grey wool, darned at one end, and it smells faintly of ink and of the man who wore it. He wraps the vial in it twice and wedges it upright in the satchel between two of the red flasks, padded so glass can't knock on glass. The hat stays alone on its peg, next to the stretched empty space.

The box stays where it is, on the far corner of the table, square to the edge. Nobody has touched the grey dust on its lid, and the light from the front windows lies flat across the green.

Pell leans over the head of the stair and sends his voice down, quiet and level. The narrow stairwell carries it to the street door.

In the room behind him the lamp glass is black, the pen still lies across the closed inkpot, and the oilcloth's waxed-string marks are left on the table where the bundle was. Down in the yard the mallet doesn't start up again.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I stay at the threshold, looking at the box without touching it.

“Pell. Vell showed us brown wax. That seal’s green. Is the mark the same?”

I call softly down the stair, “Sefa, come have a look when you’re ready.”

Then I ask Pell, “Anything else out of place?”

scenes.narration:
Bram stays on the threshold with his shield arm against the doorframe. The boards of the room start just in front of his boots and he keeps them clean. He speaks his questions into the room, towards Pell, keeping his voice low the way you do in a dead man's house. Then he turns his head and sends the call down the stair. The narrow well takes it down to the street door, the same way it brought every word up.

From where he stands he can see the room for himself.

The box sits on the far corner of the table, squared to the edge, about the size of a loaf tin. Even from the door he can see the green. It's deep bottle green, not the brown drop Vell pressed on the counter, and there's a dull grey disc under the wax across the join of the lid. From this distance he can't make out what's stamped into it, whether it's a ring with a V or anything else. That would take a closer look than the threshold gives him. The light from the two front windows lies flat across the lid and its fine grey dust, and nothing has disturbed the dust.

The rest of the room is what ten years of camp and inn rooms have taught him to read. The bed is made, with the blanket folded square. The chair stands pushed back from the table at an angle, the way it ends up once a man has been lifted out of it. The lamp glass is black with soot. A pen lies across a capped inkpot. The grate in the side wall is full of grey ash, which is a lot of ash for a mild spring night, just as Wenna said. A bitter smell still hangs under the lye and old smoke, sharp enough to catch at the back of his throat. By the bed a stool stands with a small clean circle in the dust on its seat, where something stood until recently. On the boards just below it is a dried brownish ring the size of a palm. By the door, a hat hangs alone on its peg. The wood of the peg beside it is stretched and empty, as if it held something heavy for a long time.

Through the front windows he can see roof shingles across the lane and a flat white morning sky with smithy smoke drifting under it. Down in the yard the mallet is silent.

Sefa goes up on the edges of the treads. The old pine takes her weight with no more than a sigh. Behind her at the foot of the stair, Wenna has moved onto the bottom step, one hand on the newel post and the key ring hanging from the other. She doesn't follow. "I'll be *here*," she says up the well, to nobody in particular, and folds her arms.

The landing is small and smells of lye and old timber. Sefa stops at the open door with one hand on the jamb. A man in chain mail already fills most of the threshold, so she sees the room past his shoulder.

The box is there. It's the first thing she finds, because it's the only thing in the room that looks like it was put down on purpose: an iron-bound oak box about the size of a loaf tin, squared to the far corner of the table under the front windows. Its seal is deep bottle green, not Vell's brown, with a dull grey disc under the wax across the join of the lid. From the door she can't make out what's pressed into it. The fine grey dust lies evenly over the lid, and nothing has wiped or smudged it. The padlock hangs closed on its hasp. If Brannock found a quieter door into this room, it wasn't through that box.

The rest of the room reaches her a piece at a time. The bed is made with the blanket squared at its foot. The chair sits pushed back from the table at an angle. The lamp glass is black. The back shutter over the yard is shut flat with a peg through its hasp, the way Wenna said. By the bed a stool stands bare, with a small clean circle in the dust on its seat where something stood until recently. On the boards below it there's a brownish ring the size of a palm.

The smell reaches her last, and she knows it before she thinks about it. It's bitter and green under the lye and the cold smoke, and it catches at the back of the throat. It's the smell of the locked cupboard at the end of the hospice ward, where the sisters kept the drops measured out by the spoon. She smelled it every night of the fever. The trouble with that cupboard was that what was in it could help you or kill you, depending on the dose, and the smell was the same either way.

Down in the yard the mallet stays silent. Below her, Wenna shifts her weight on the bottom step, and the stair gives one small creak.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell waits a breath at the head of the stair for an answer. None comes, and the mallet in the yard stays quiet. That bothers him more than any noise would.

He pulls the door to behind him, not latched, just enough that the box can't be seen from the stairwell. He keeps Wenna's key in his fist rather than his pocket. Then he goes down the stair the way he came up, on the edges of the treads, one hand on the wall. He stops at the last turn, where he can see the street door and the foot of the stair before anyone down there sees him.

He looks for who's standing where: Bram, Sefa, Wenna, Tobin at the gate, and anyone who doesn't belong. He listens before he shows himself. If it's only the three of them and some bit of news the child brought, he comes down the last steps easy and keeps his voice low.

"The little one. Who sent her, and what was the message?"

If someone else is at that door, a brown coat or a Fist tabard, he stays where he is, out of sight on the turn, with his right hand resting near the shortsword hilt. He lets Bram do the talking and listens to every word.

Either way, he doesn't mention the bundle or the vial in front of Wenna or Tobin.

Out of game: I'd like to know what the child said, and whether Bram and Sefa stayed at the door on purpose. Then I'll bring them up to the room. Also, could Pell make any guess at the script on the matrix handle, or at what a closed eye over scales stands for (a god, a house, a guild)? An Intelligence or History check is fine if that fits.

scenes.narration:
Pell waits at the head of the stair for one breath, then a second. No answer comes up the well. Down in the yard the mallet is still silent.

He reaches back and pulls the door of Jassan's room to. He doesn't latch it, just closes it far enough that the table and the green seal can't be seen from the stair. Wenna's iron key stays in his fist with the worn bow against his palm. Then he goes down the way he came up, on the edges of the treads with one hand flat to the wall. The cold weight in his inner pocket shifts against his ribs at every step.

He stops partway down and tries to place the matrix in his head: the scales with level pans, the sleeper's eye, and the hooks and strokes on the handle that his eye kept sliding off.

He goes through what he knows, and none of it fits. In the Gate scales hang over every moneychanger's door from the Wide down to the docks, painted, carved or hammered out of tin. They belong to every counting-room and to none in particular. A closed eye means nothing to him at all. No crew used it, no house he ever robbed had it, and no shrine he walked past showed it. The letters on the handle are no cant and no script he has seen on a door or a ledger. All he knows of the mark is what he saw at the table, and the matrix stays as strange in his pocket as it was under the board.

At the last turn he stops where the wall still hides him and looks down the rest of the stair before anyone below can look up.

Wenna stands on the bottom step with one hand on the newel post and the key ring hanging from the other. Her face is turned up the stair. Through the street door he can see a slice of the lane in flat morning light, the grey planks of the gate, and Tobin at the gatepost with his mallet hanging from one hand. There's no brown coat at the door and no Fist tabard, and nobody stands in the lane who wasn't there before.

Bram and Sefa aren't at the foot of the stair. They're on it, coming up. The man in chain mail is in front, keeping to the edges of the treads the way he was told, and Sefa is a few steps behind him. The old pine sighs under the iron rings.

Pell comes down off the turn to meet them halfway and keeps his voice under the creak of the wood. "The little one. Who sent her, and what was the message?"

He doesn't say a word about the bundle or the vial. Below them Wenna watches the key in his fist and doesn't come up. Out at the gate Tobin shifts his weight and stays put.

 Pell tried to name the mark, and he couldn't. Neither the scales, the sleeper's eye nor the hooked letters on the handle connect to anything he learned on the roofs of the Wide or anywhere since. He goes on down the stair knowing no more about the matrix than he did when he lifted it out of the hollow.

Your narration:
<<<
Pell waits at the head of the stair for one breath, then a second. No answer comes up the well. Down in the yard the mallet is still silent.

He reaches back and pulls the door of Jassan's room to. He doesn't latch it, just closes it far enough that the table and the green seal can't be seen from the stair. Wenna's iron key stays in his fist with the worn bow against his palm. Then he goes down the way he came up, on the edges of the treads with one hand flat to the wall. The cold weight in his inner pocket shifts against his ribs at every step.

He stops partway down and tries to place the matrix in his head: the scales with level pans, the sleeper's eye, and the hooks and strokes on the handle that his eye kept sliding off.

He goes through what he knows, and none of it fits. In the Gate scales hang over every moneychanger's door from the Wide down to the docks, painted, carved or hammered out of tin. They belong to every counting-room and to none in particular. A closed eye means nothing to him at all. No crew used it, no house he ever robbed had it, and no shrine he walked past showed it. The letters on the handle are no cant and no script he has seen on a door or a ledger. All he knows of the mark is what he saw at the table, and the matrix stays as strange in his pocket as it was under the board.

At the last turn he stops where the wall still hides him and looks down the rest of the stair before anyone below can look up.

Wenna stands on the bottom step with one hand on the newel post and the key ring hanging from the other. Her face is turned up the stair. Through the street door he can see a slice of the lane in flat morning light, the grey planks of the gate, and Tobin at the gatepost with his mallet hanging from one hand. There's no brown coat at the door and no Fist tabard, and nobody stands in the lane who wasn't there before.

Bram and Sefa aren't at the foot of the stair. They're on it, coming up. The man in chain mail is in front, keeping to the edges of the treads the way he was told, and Sefa is a few steps behind him. The old pine sighs under the iron rings.

Pell comes down off the turn to meet them halfway and keeps his voice under the creak of the wood. "The little one. Who sent her, and what was the message?"

He doesn't say a word about the bundle or the vial. Below them Wenna watches the key in his fist and doesn't come up. Out at the gate Tobin shifts his weight and stays put.

He goes on down the stair knowing no more about the matrix than he did when he lifted it out of the hollow.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa doesn't step over the threshold. She stands at the jamb and breathes once through her mouth, steadying herself.

"The smell." Her voice is still low, meant for the two of them, but there's no question in it now. "I know it. Poppy, or something near it — the kind they measure in drops. The hospice kept it locked at the end of the ward. A spoonful or two helps; too much stops the heart gentle as sleep. A man could sit down in his chair and not get up." She lets that settle. "That would look like a heart that stopped. Especially if no one looked too long."

She glances once at the green seal, the dust, the clean circle on the stool. "And the fire, the barred shutter, the man asking was the seal whole — he wasn't only watching the house. He was making sure no one found it first."

Then, quieter, her eyes move to the top of the stair: "Wenna's at the bottom step and she won't want to hear that word. But if this room's a death by poison, the strongbox isn't our only errand any more."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stops two treads above Bram, close enough to whisper, and waits for the answer about the child before he says anything else. Then he tips his head up the stair.

"Up. Quick and quiet. I'll tell you on the way."

Back in the room, he shuts the door properly this time and puts his back to it. He keeps his voice down so it won't carry through the boards to Wenna.

"Short version. The box's seal isn't Vell's. Green wax over lead, a mark of scales with a closed eye over them. Nobody's broken it. And the stamp that made it was under that board." He touches his jerkin over the inner pocket, but doesn't take the bundle out. "So Jassan was sealing boxes for someone besides Vell. And he was writing to a Fist sergeant about notes sold before some wagons, and then the letter went in the fire. Then his heart stopped." He nods at the dried ring on the floor. "The vial's in my satchel, wrapped. Sefa, I'd like you to smell the stain and look at the vial. Don't open it. And look at that wax. If there's anything you can do to tell whether it's warded or trapped, do it before Bram lifts it."

He looks between the two of them.

"Here's where I come out. We were hired to bring Vell a sealed box, and that's a sealed box. We take it to him whole and let him explain why it isn't sealed in his wax. Brannock asked twice whether the seal was whole. That tells me the seal matters more than the ledgers, and I don't want it opened on our watch, by us or anyone." A beat. "But I'm not handing Vell the stamp yet. That's ours to bargain with until we know who Master Thale is and what Jassan was frightened of."

He glances at the front window. "Brannock's due before midday, and he chalked that gate. I'd rather be gone with the box before he's back, and not down the front stair past him in the lane if we can help it. Bram, can you carry it wrapped in the blanket off the bed, so it doesn't look like a strongbox in the street?"

Out of game: I'm keeping Wenna's key until we leave, and I'll hand it back on the way out. If Sefa has Detect Magic or something like it, I'd like her to use it on the wax and the matrix.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Something’s been taken off that stool,” I say quietly, pointing out the clean circle and the dried ring beneath it. “And perhaps off the peg. Could be ordinary enough, but worth asking Wenna.”

I stay clear of Pell’s work and look back down the stair, listening for anyone arriving below.

“Let’s establish whose seal that is before we move the box. Vell was quite particular.”

scenes.narration:
Pell's question about the child hangs in the stairwell for a breath, and neither of the other two answers it. Sefa is at the jamb with her eyes on the room, and Bram is turned to look past his own shoulder at the stair. So Pell goes up the last two treads and past them. The man in chain mail fills the doorway, and Pell has to turn sideways to get by him. He reaches back for the door.

It won't close. Bram is standing in it with his shield arm against the frame, and Sefa's hand is on the jamb. Pell ends up just inside with his back to the wall next to the door, close enough that all three of them can keep their voices low. The door stays open behind them, onto the landing and the stairwell, the same stairwell that has carried every word up from the street all morning.

Sefa speaks first, quietly and without any doubt in her voice. Pell speaks after her, and he goes through it fast: the green wax, the lead, the scales and the closed eye, the stamp under the board, the letter to the Fist sergeant, the vial wrapped in his satchel. Bram points out the clean ring on the stool and the stretched empty peg, then turns his head back toward the stair to listen.

Nobody is coming up. The street door shows the same slice of lane, the grey gate, flat morning light. Nobody new is on the step.

Wenna is still on the bottom step, but she isn't looking at the key anymore.

Wenna is watching the top of the stair now. She can tell they're talking up there, three voices low and close together, but the creak of the old pine and the noise from the lane drown out the words before they get down to her.

"You're a long while *looking*," she calls up. She isn't sharp about it. She's a landlady who has a key out and a dead man's room open. "I've the step to do before dinner."

Out at the gate, Tobin has hung the mallet from his belt by its handle, freeing his hands. He stands with his arms crossed over his apron, watching the lane toward the high street, the way Brannock left last night.

In the room, the light from the front windows lies flat across the green seal. Under the lye and the cold smoke, the bitter smell still rises off the dried ring on the boards.

messages.text:
Pell leans out past Bram's shoulder and calls down to Wenna, easy and apologetic.

"Nearly done, mistress. A dead man's room, we're being careful with it. You'll have your key and your step back in a few minutes."

Then he turns back, low, under the creak of the stair.

"Sefa's right. That's no heart, that's murder, and Vell's man from the Fist wrote it down as a heart." He glances at the box. "So here's how I'd run the day. The box goes to Vell, sealed, like we were paid for. We watch his face when he sees green wax instead of brown, because that tells us whether he knew. Then the Song of the Morning, to see if the key's still on that cord round Jassan's neck. Then the garrison, to find Sergeant Cowl and ask him what letter he never got." A beat. "Nobody here says *poison* aloud, to Wenna or to Vell. Not yet."

He crosses to the bed, picks up the folded blanket from its foot and holds it ready, still not touching the box.

"Sefa, can you tell if that wax has anything *on* it? A ward, a mark, anything that would know if it moved? If you can't, say so and Bram lifts it slow. Better that than walking it into the street and finding out the hard way." He looks at Bram. "Wrap it in this. Carry it like bedding, not like a strongbox. Front stair, since the back's only shutters and a lean-to and we're not climbing out with a box in daylight. But we go up the lane the other way from the high street, the way Brannock *didn't* go, and loop round to Vell's."

On the way out, he'll give the iron key back into Wenna's hand himself, with a nod and a "Thank you, mistress, truly."

Out of game: Does Sefa have Detect Magic or anything similar? If she does, I'd like her to cast it on the box before Bram lifts it. If not, Bram lifts it carefully, wrapped in the blanket.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I step fully into the room, clearing the doorway so Pell can close it.

“Still checking, Mistress Pike,” I call down. “We’ll return your key when we’re done.”

Then, quietly to Pell: “I missed some of that. What stamp under which board? And what does the letter to the sergeant say?”

I keep my hands off the box. “We were hired for Vell’s seal. This isn’t it. If there’s evidence Ferr was poisoned, we need to hear that letter before deciding where the box goes.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa keeps her voice low, her gaze moving from the green seal to Pell and Bram in turn.

"Then we do exactly what we were hired for — carry it to Vell now, seal whole — and we tell him plainly it isn't his mark on it. Green wax over lead, scales and a shut eye. He can call it whatever he likes, but not broken by us."

She looks at Pell. "Keep the vial, and the stamp if you've got it. If it's still back under the board, don't leave it here. Those aren't Vell's; they're proof Jassan didn't simply stop breathing in his chair, and that letter's proof there's a sergeant somewhere in this who may already be bought."

Then to Bram: "You carry the box and go first down the stair. If the old wood's going to complain, let it complain under you." The corner of her mouth lifts, but it isn't humour. "Pell, put the room back as close as you can — board down, nothing moving. I'll take the rear so we all come down together."

She leans a little toward the stairwell and calls down, easily, as if the morning were ordinary: "Mistress Pike, we've found it. We're bringing it down now, and you'll have your key back the moment we're off your stair."

scenes.narration:
Bram steps over the threshold and onto the boards. Old floorboards take chain mail badly. The one by the door groans under his weight, the next one answers it, and he stops a long pace inside with his hands well clear of the table. The doorway behind him is open now. Sefa stands in it with one hand still on the jamb. Nobody has shut the door yet.

Pell leans out past where Bram's shoulder used to be and sends his easy apology down the stairwell. Bram calls down a moment later, *still checking*, and Sefa, from the jamb, follows with *we've found it, we're bringing it down now.*

There's a short silence from the bottom step.

"*Found* it." Wenna's voice comes up the well, dry as lye. "It's not been *lost*, love. It's been sat on his table three days. Checking or bringing, the three of you, make your minds up between you and tell me the one." The key ring jingles once. "I'm not going anywhere. That's the trouble."

Out at the gatepost, Tobin turns his head toward the house and then goes back to watching the lane.

Inside, the talk goes low again. Pell has the blanket off the foot of the bed, folded square the way Jassan left it, and holds it over his forearm like a tailor holding cloth. He hasn't gone any nearer the box. Bram's questions hang in the room: *what stamp, under which board, what does the letter say.* The burnt paper is still flat inside the cover of Pell's tool roll, and Bram hasn't seen a word of it. Sefa has said her piece: to Vell now, seal whole, and tell him straight it isn't his mark. Pell asked whether there's anything on the wax. Nobody has answered him yet, and Sefa hasn't moved from the jamb.

The box hasn't moved either. It sits square to the corner of the table in the window light. The dust on the green lies even. The padlock hangs shut. Bram stands closest to it now, closer than anyone has been except Pell. From here the stamp shows through the thin skin of wax over the lead: a pair of scales with level pans, and above them a closed eye drawn as one curve with lashes. There's no ring and no V.

Somewhere up toward the high street a temple bell starts ringing the hour, slow and bright over the smithy hammers. It strikes ten and stops. In the yard below, Tobin's mallet stays on its barrel head.

 (Out of game: Sefa's sheet has no Detect Magic, and her player didn't declare a spell. Pell asked her to check the wax, and only her player can answer or act on that, so I didn't play it.)

(Out of game: Pell's question about a ward on the wax was asked in the story, and it stays open until Sefa's player answers it.)

(Out of game: Pell suggested that Bram lift the box and wrap it, but Bram's player didn't declare it, and Bram said he wants to hear the letter before deciding where the box goes. That's Bram's player's call, so the box stays on the table.)

(Out of game: Pell and Sefa want to leave now and Bram doesn't yet, and nobody has the box, so nobody has gone down the stair. Pell giving Wenna back her key on the way out waits for the same reason.)

The rules:
- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.
- Add nothing beyond your narration and the players' messages. Never reveal what only the game master knows.
- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.
- Write the screens in the order you are asked for them.

Then say who is where at the end of it: group the characters who are together (can see and hear each other) — every character in this scene in exactly one group; a character from elsewhere who, by your narration, is now with them joins their group — and name each one's place in a few words.
Then say who is waiting at the end of it: a character in this scene who is asleep, unconscious, or has said they wait for something named (until dawn, until another comes back) and has nothing to decide until it comes — with what ends the wait, in a few words. A character with anything to decide is never waiting.
