messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Song first,” I say quietly. “It’s ten. Vell gave us till nightfall, and the temple’s holding Ferr’s body and perhaps his key. Odda’s there till midday too. We can see her without opening the box or breaking our agreement.”

I look to Pell. “And I still need to hear what that letter says. Not just the plan.”

I accept the blanket, leaving the seal visible as I carefully wrap the box’s sides and base. If neither of them warns me of a danger in lifting it, I lift it gently, keeping it level.

“We’ll keep it sealed. But I want those questions answered before we put it in Vell’s hands.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa doesn't step past the threshold yet. She answers Pell in a murmur, still watching the box.

"No Detect Magic. I can't tell a ward by eye, and the Lantern didn't make me a seer." Then, more like herself: "But I can read what's written, in any tongue. If there are words cut into that lead or pressed into the wax, I'll have them."

She steps inside, just far enough to stand beside the table, and folds her hands behind her back so there's no chance of brushing the box. She bends a little, letting the window light rake the green seal and the grey disc, and studies the mark — the level scales, the closed eye — for letters, initials, a minting cut, anything at all.

After a pause she straightens. "I don't know the sign. If it's a house mark, it's not one I've seen in the Gate. If it's a god's, it's not one my sisters taught." She glances at Bram. "Let's not make a catechism out of it here. Lift it the way Pell said, slow, blanket under and folded over, and keep it level like it might be full of live coals — not because I saw a ward, but because a sealed devil-box from a dead man's table is the sort of thing you carry carefully all the way to the man who says it's his."

She moves back to the doorway and turns to face the stair, ready to go down last. "And Bram — it goes all the way to Vell. No detours to the Song, no widow, no garrison, not with it in your hands. Put it on his counter first, seal up, and let him see the green."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell slides the tool roll out of his jerkin, opens the cover and holds it flat under Bram's nose so the burnt curl stays still in the light.

"That's the letter. *To Sergeant Cowl of the Fist, at the garrison.* All that's left is *the notes were sold before the wagons.* The rest went in the grate." He closes the cover over it again. "The stamp was under the board by the bed, wrapped in oilcloth with a stub of the same green wax. It's the scales and the closed eye, and it made that seal. I've got it. Vell doesn't need to know that yet."

He leans to the door and calls down, warm and plain:

"Bringing it, mistress. Two minutes, and your key's back in your hand."

Then, low again: "Ten o'clock. Brannock said before midday. We decide where it goes on the street, not in here." He doesn't wait for anyone to argue. If Sefa had a spell for the wax, she'd have said so.

Pell lifts the box himself. He's the one who finds tripwires for a living. scenes.narration:
Pell opens the tool roll under Bram's nose and holds it flat so the burnt curl stays still in the window light. Bram can read the top line for himself, in a small careful hand: *To Sergeant Cowl of the Fist, at the garrison —*. Below it, between the scorched hole and the black lace, is the one line Pell reads out. Then the cover closes over it again. Pell tells him the rest in a few words: the board by the bed, the oilcloth, the stamp that made that seal, the stub of the same green wax.

Sefa answers him from the jamb before she steps in. She has no spell for wards. She can read whatever is written there. She crosses to the table with her hands clasped behind her back and bends until the light from the front windows rakes across the green.

There's nothing for her to read. No letters are cut into the lead, nothing is pressed into the wax, and there's no initial or minting mark at the rim. There are only the level scales and the closed eye with its lashes. With the light lying low across it she can see something Bram couldn't from the door. Deep in the green, a fine grain of rings sits close and even around the stamp, like ripples around a dropped stone. They aren't writing. Her eyes find nothing in them to read. She straightens, says what she has to say, and goes back to the doorway, facing the stair.

Bram takes the blanket off Pell's forearm. While he shakes it out of its square, Pell crouches at the table edge and sights along the underside of the box, then the shackle of the padlock, then the hasp. He finds no thread and no pin, and nothing ties the iron bands to the wood. The box just sits on the table. Nobody warns Bram of anything.

So Bram lifts it. It's heavier than a loaf tin has any right to be, and the paper inside shifts once with a dull, solid slide. He keeps it level the whole way. He wraps the wool around the sides and under the base and leaves the lid bare, so the green seal sits uncovered in the middle of the bundle and nothing rubs at it. The dust on the lid stays even.

(Out of game: you both declared the lift. In this round's order Bram's came first, so Bram lifted the box; Pell's check of the underside came before it.)

Pell leans out to the stairwell and calls down that they're bringing it. He gives the room one last look: the board seated, the chair where Jassan's chair was left, nothing of theirs on the table. Then they go down in a line on the edges of the treads, Bram first with the box held against his mail, Sefa behind him, Pell last. The old pine complains under Bram the whole way, just as Sefa said it would.

Wenna is off the bottom step before they reach it. She looks at the bundle first and only then at the faces.

Pell puts the iron key into her hand and closes her fingers over it. She hears him out, the thanks and then the quieter part, and her chin comes up.

"Tell him Vell's people took it. Well, that's the *truth*, so I'll tell him that, and gladly." She hangs the key back on its ring without looking. "I'll be honest with you, I don't owe that man anything. But if he asks me where you went, I'll say I didn't see, and that's true as well, because I'll be doing my step." Then her eyes go back to the bundle in Bram's arms, and her mouth thins. "That's the *room's* blanket. Not Jassan's, mine, it goes with the bed. You bring it back when you've done carrying, or it's four silver, and I'm not joking." She looks Bram in the face to make sure he knows it.

Tobin has stepped back from the gatepost to let them through. He says nothing about the bundle and nothing about the box. He glances once up the lane toward the high street and once down it. "Clear," he says.

The chalk mark on the left post is still there at knee height, bright and unscuffed.

Out in the Coast Way the morning has gone fully grey-white. Smoke from the smithies drifts low over the roofs, and the charcoal handcart still stands by the farrier's with nobody at its shafts. Pell has already turned the other way from the high street, toward the lower end of the lane where the houses thin out and a back way runs off behind the chandler's yards, and he's talking low as he walks. Up the other way, past the chandler's corner where the runner girl vanished, the high street leads toward the temple bell that struck ten a few minutes ago. Bram stands in the gateway with the box against his chest, the green seal bare to the sky. Sefa is a step behind him, and the three of them are already a little apart.

Behind them Wenna stands on her step with her rag, and doesn't start on it yet.

While he shakes it out of its square, Pell crouches at the table edge and sights along the underside of the box, then the shackle of the padlock, then the hasp. He finds no thread and no pin, and nothing ties the iron bands to the wood. The box just sits on the table. Nobody warns Bram of anything.

So Bram lifts it. It's heavier than a loaf tin has any right to be, and the paper inside shifts once with a dull, solid slide. He keeps it level the whole way. He wraps the wool around the sides and under the base and leaves the lid bare, so the green seal sits uncovered in the middle of the bundle and nothing rubs at it. The dust on the lid stays even.

Pell leans out to the stairwell and calls down that they're bringing it. He gives the room one last look: the board seated, the chair where Jassan's chair was left, nothing of theirs on the table. Then they go down in a line on the edges of the treads, Bram first with the box held against his mail, Sefa behind him, Pell last. The old pine complains under Bram the whole way, just as Sefa said it would.

Wenna is off the bottom step before they reach it. She looks at the bundle first and only then at the faces.

Pell puts the iron key into her hand and closes her fingers over it. She hears him out, the thanks and then the quieter part, and her chin comes up.

"Tell him Vell's people took it. Well, that's the *truth*, so I'll tell him that, and gladly." She hangs the key back on its ring without looking. "I'll be honest with you, I don't owe that man anything. But if he asks me where you went, I'll say I didn't see, and that's true as well, because I'll be doing my step." Then her eyes go back to the bundle in Bram's arms, and her mouth thins. "That's the *room's* blanket. Not Jassan's, mine, it goes with the bed. You bring it back when you've done carrying, or it's four silver, and I'm not joking." She looks Bram in the face to make sure he knows it.

Tobin has stepped back from the gatepost to let them through. He says nothing about the bundle and nothing about the box. He glances once up the lane toward the high street and once down it. "Clear," he says.

The chalk mark on the left post is still there at knee height, bright and unscuffed.

Out in the Coast Way the morning has gone fully grey-white. Smoke from the smithies drifts low over the roofs, and the charcoal handcart still stands by the farrier's with nobody at its shafts. Pell has already turned the other way from the high street, toward the lower end of the lane where the houses thin out and a back way runs off behind the chandler's yards, and he's talking low as he walks. Up the other way, past the chandler's corner where the runner girl vanished, the high street leads toward the temple bell that struck ten a few minutes ago. Bram stands in the gateway with the box against his chest, the green seal bare to the sky. Sefa is a step behind him, and the three of them are already a little apart.

Behind them Wenna stands on her step with her rag, and doesn't start on it yet.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa touches Wenna's arm once, not lingering, and lowers her voice.

"You've done right by him. Keep your door on the latch till we're clear, and let Tobin watch the lane." A glance at the box in Bram's arms. "The blanket comes back before night. I'll bring it myself, if I'm the one still walking."

Then she steps out of the gate after Pell, keeping just behind Bram's shield-side, and answers Pell without turning: "Back lanes, yes. If Brannock's already come back from his business, I'd rather he find an empty stair than three hirelings with their arms full."

As they move, she lets her eyes sweep the lane behind and the mouths of the little alleys. Her voice stays low, meant for the two of them only. "Vell hears the plain truth first: the box was waiting as you say, but it carries a green seal over lead, scales and a shut eye — not his mark. Let him reach for it himself and see his own face. The stamp, the vial, the letter... those can wait in your pockets for the moment they're worth more than silver."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell catches up to Bram in two quick steps and drops his voice under the smithy noise. He doesn't stop walking.

"Bram. You said *Odda until midday*. Who's Odda? Was that what the little runner brought?" He glances back once at the chalked gatepost, then forward again. "If the Song buries Jassan at midday, the key on his neck goes into the ground with him, and we lose it."

He looks from one to the other and settles it fast.

"Then we're both right, and we don't stand in the lane arguing about it with a sealed box out in the open. Sefa's right that the box goes to Vell now, seal up, before Brannock comes sniffing. Bram's right that the Song can't wait. So I'll split it. You two take the box straight to Vell by the back way. Sefa, you tell him it isn't his mark, and watch his face when you do. Don't mention the stamp or the vial. Get the fee, and get the four gold on Wenna's receipt." He nods at the paper inside Bram's coat. "I'm the quick one. I'll run to the Song, find this Odda, and ask after the cord before they close the ground. Then I'll meet you outside Vell's. If I'm not there by the time the bell rings eleven, come to the temple."

He taps Bram's arm where the blanket's corner hangs. "And that's Wenna's blanket. Four silver, or we take it back. Don't let Vell keep it."

If they agree, Pell peels off at the next gap between houses and cuts up toward the high street and the temple bell at a fast, unremarkable walk. He keeps to the shady side and checks the chandler's corner for a waiting brown coat before he turns it.

Out of game: if Bram or Sefa object to splitting up, Pell goes with the group to Vell's first and then on to the Song. I'd still like to know who Odda is and what the child's message was.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“You’ll get your blanket back, Mistress Pike.”

I follow Pell far enough to clear the gate, then speak low to both companions.

“If we’re going straight to Vell, I need to buy Odda’s note before we hand over the box. Forty gold saves her house. I counted my purse badly upstairs—I’ve not quite twenty-five.”

I look between them. “Will either of you lend me sixteen gold against my share of the fee? You get it back at the counter today. I’ll buy the note first, then we deliver the box together and ask him about that seal. No opening it, no hiding papers.”

I keep the bundle level against my chest. “That’s why I asked for the temple first. I won’t pretend this is only about Ferr’s key.”

scenes.narration:
Wenna looks down at the hand on her arm as if she isn't sure what it's doing there. Then she lets it stay the moment it stays.

"On the latch. In the *morning*." She sniffs, but she doesn't push the hand away. "If I'm the one still walking, she says. Over a box of sums." She looks at Sefa a moment longer, and the tartness goes out of her face. "Well. You bring that blanket yourself, then, and I'll put the kettle on for it. Go on."

Bram tells her over his shoulder that she'll get it back. She answers with a short nod at the blanket in his arms rather than at him, and the rag finally goes to work on the step. Tobin hasn't moved from inside the gate. His eyes are on the lane toward the high street, and he lifts his chin once to Sefa as she passes. That's all she gets from him.

---

The lower end of the Coast Way thins out fast. After the last house with washing out, a cart track runs off between a chandler's back fence and a row of tumbledown sheds. It's rutted and muddy at the edges and smells of tallow and wet straw. The noise of the smithies comes from the far side of the roofs here, muffled to a steady clanging that you feel more than hear.

Pell's two quick steps bring him level with Bram's elbow. He asks his questions under the hammering and lays the split out between one stride and the next. Nobody stops walking. Nobody says yes to it either. Sefa has already answered the part about the back lanes, and Bram answers with a plan of his own. So when they reach the first gap between two sheds, a narrow slot of daylight leading up toward the high street and the temple bell, Pell doesn't turn into it. He goes past it with the others, and the box goes past it in Bram's arms.

Bram says his piece low and plain, with the bundle held level against his mail. Pell gets his answer about Odda in it, though not in the order he asked: a note, forty gold, a house, and a woman who wants it bought back before the box goes home. Bram doesn't ask anybody to act surprised, and he doesn't hide that the temple was never only about the key.

While the men talk, Sefa keeps half a step behind Bram's shield side and watches the track behind them. Nothing in the lane bothers her eye. A woman at the chandler's back door is scraping a tallow pot into a bucket and doesn't look up. Two boys are throwing a stick for a yellow dog in the ruts and only stop to stare at the chain mail. A carter is backing a dray of charcoal sacks into a shed and swearing at his mule as if he means it personally. Nobody falls in behind them. Nobody stands at the mouth of the Coast Way to watch them go. Back there, the chalk mark is still on its gatepost at knee height, and from here the gate has gone out of sight behind the sheds.

The box is heavy. It doesn't get any lighter for being carried carefully, and Bram feels it now in his forearms, a dead square weight with the papers inside shifting once at a rut. The green seal sits bare to the flat white sky in its nest of wool. The dust on it hasn't been touched.

Ahead, the track forks at a stone water trough where a farrier's boy is filling buckets. Left, it runs on behind the yards, a long loop round the backs of the high-street houses toward Vell's end of town, with Vell's counting-house somewhere beyond. Right, a cobbled alley climbs between two smithies straight to the high street. At its top, over the roofs, you can see the gilded sunburst on the bell tower of the Song of the Morning. A thin line of smoke comes up behind it, and it isn't a forge's.

The farrier's boy lets the bucket overflow while he gawps at the shield, then swears and pours half of it back.

Your narration:
<<<
Wenna looks down at the hand on her arm as if she isn't sure what it's doing there. Then she lets it stay the moment it stays.

"On the latch. In the *morning*." She sniffs, but she doesn't push the hand away. "If I'm the one still walking, she says. Over a box of sums." She looks at Sefa a moment longer, and the tartness goes out of her face. "Well. You bring that blanket yourself, then, and I'll put the kettle on for it. Go on."

Bram tells her over his shoulder that she'll get it back. She answers with a short nod at the blanket in his arms rather than at him, and the rag finally goes to work on the step. Tobin hasn't moved from inside the gate. His eyes are on the lane toward the high street, and he lifts his chin once to Sefa as she passes. That's all she gets from him.

---

The lower end of the Coast Way thins out fast. After the last house with washing out, a cart track runs off between a chandler's back fence and a row of tumbledown sheds. It's rutted and muddy at the edges and smells of tallow and wet straw. The noise of the smithies comes from the far side of the roofs here, muffled to a steady clanging that you feel more than hear.

Pell's two quick steps bring him level with Bram's elbow. He asks his questions under the hammering and lays the split out between one stride and the next. Nobody stops walking. Nobody says yes to it either. Sefa has already answered the part about the back lanes, and Bram answers with a plan of his own. So when they reach the first gap between two sheds, a narrow slot of daylight leading up toward the high street and the temple bell, Pell doesn't turn into it. He goes past it with the others, and the box goes past it in Bram's arms.

Bram says his piece low and plain, with the bundle held level against his mail. Pell gets his answer about Odda in it, though not in the order he asked: a note, forty gold, a house, and a woman who wants it bought back before the box goes home. Bram doesn't ask anybody to act surprised, and he doesn't hide that the temple was never only about the key.

While the men talk, Sefa keeps half a step behind Bram's shield side and watches the track behind them. Nothing in the lane bothers her eye. A woman at the chandler's back door is scraping a tallow pot into a bucket and doesn't look up. Two boys are throwing a stick for a yellow dog in the ruts and only stop to stare at the chain mail. A carter is backing a dray of charcoal sacks into a shed and swearing at his mule as if he means it personally. Nobody falls in behind them. Nobody stands at the mouth of the Coast Way to watch them go. Back there, the chalk mark is still on its gatepost at knee height, and from here the gate has gone out of sight behind the sheds.

The box is heavy. It doesn't get any lighter for being carried carefully, and Bram feels it now in his forearms, a dead square weight with the papers inside shifting once at a rut. The green seal sits bare to the flat white sky in its nest of wool. The dust on it hasn't been touched.

Ahead, the track forks at a stone water trough where a farrier's boy is filling buckets. Left, it runs on behind the yards, a long loop round the backs of the high-street houses toward Vell's end of town, with Vell's counting-house somewhere beyond. Right, a cobbled alley climbs between two smithies straight to the high street. At its top, over the roofs, you can see the gilded sunburst on the bell tower of the Song of the Morning. A thin line of smoke comes up behind it, and it isn't a forge's.

The farrier's boy lets the bucket overflow while he gawps at the shield, then swears and pours half of it back.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stops at the trough, out of the farrier's boy's earshot, and puts a hand flat on the blanket over the box, holding Bram there a moment.

"Hold on. You keep saying Odda, and I still don't know who she is." He keeps it low and quick. "Whose note is it, who holds it, and where is she? At the Song?" A beat, and his eyes narrow. "Jassan wrote *the notes were sold before the wagons*. If her note is one of those, and it's sitting in a moneylender's drawer, I want to know whose drawer before I put my coin in it. Vell's? Or this Master Thale's?"

He doesn't make Bram beg for it. "Sixteen's most of what I've got left after Wenna. Tell me straight and I'll lend it against your share, paid back at Vell's counter today. I'm not asking for interest. I'm asking not to be lied to." He glances at Sefa. "If that's fair by you too."

Then he looks up the cobbled alley at the gilded sunburst and the thin line of smoke behind it.

"And that settles the road. If Odda's at the Song until midday and Jassan's lying there with a cord round his neck, we go right, all three of us, box and all. We don't split it." He tips his chin at the smoke. "That smoke isn't a forge. I want to know what's burning before we walk in carrying a sealed box. Bram, keep the seal against your chest, not facing the street. I'll go first up the alley and look at the top before you two come out of it."

If Bram answers and it holds together, Pell counts sixteen gold into his palm right there, out of sight behind the bulk of his mail. Then he takes the right fork up the alley, a few steps ahead, keeping to the smithy walls.

Out of game: if Bram's answer fits, Pell lends him 16 gp, which leaves him 12 gp, 2 sp, 2 ep and 55 cp. I'd like to see the top of the alley and the source of that smoke before the others step out into the high street.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I stop clear of the trough, letting the others draw close.

“Odda Brand. Harl’s widow—he was a carter lost with a train going south to Nashkel. Her signed letter came first; the runner brought word she’s waiting at the Song.”

I look to Sefa. “Can you lend me the sixteen? I need an answer before we deliver this.”

Then to Pell: “Go after Ferr’s key if you think time’s short. Don’t wait on our account. If Sefa can cover the loan, we can settle the note at Vell’s before handing him the box, as I’ve asked. If not, I’m for the Song to speak with Odda first. We still have hours to earn our fee.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stops at the fork only long enough to look both ways, then speaks low and level, in the tone she might use to stop two men at a sickbed door.

"Pell, go up to the Song now. Find the woman by the east door as the girl said, but don't spend a copper and don't promise her anything. Ask two things: what proof she has that her man's note is in this box, and whether the temple still has Jassan's cord — key and all. If they've set it aside with him, ask them to hold it till we come. Say it's for a death that ought to be looked at again."

She turns to Bram, not unkindly. "And you — we take the box by the left track, straight to Vell's counter, just as we were hired. You don't stand in the temple porch with that in your arms while Brannock or Thale's people are due back in the street. This is the one thing every one of them wants, and you're the only man carrying it."

A beat.

"As for lending: I'll help Odda if she's telling the truth, but my share of the fee isn't mine until that seal's sitting on Vell's counter. He won't call in her note while the box is still here, not unless one of us hands it to him with her name on our lips. We say nothing of her. We collect what we're owed, then we go to the widow with real coin and all three of us armed."

She nods toward the left fork. "So: the box first. The rest follows."

scenes.narration:
Pell stops them a couple of strides past the trough, where the slosh of the farrier's boy's bucket covers low voices, and lays his hand flat on the wool over the box. Bram stops.

Bram answers him: Odda Brand, Harl's widow, a carter's train lost going south, the letter first and then the runner. He asks Sefa for the sixteen, and he tells Pell to go after the key if he thinks time is short. Sefa answers both of them in her sickbed-door voice. The box goes left to Vell's, her share isn't hers to lend until the seal is on his counter, and nobody says Odda's name to Vell.

Pell hears all of it. A carter's widow, a train lost on the road to Nashkel, a forty-gold note waiting in a moneylender's box. Set beside the one line on the burnt paper in his tool roll, it fits with nothing sticking out. He turns his back to the trough, puts his shoulder into the bulk of Bram's mail so the farrier's boy sees only two backs, and counts sixteen gold pieces off the top of his purse into Bram's hand one at a time. Afterwards his purse is lighter by more than half.

Then he takes the right fork.

The alley climbs between two smithies on cobbles worn into shallow dishes. It's hot on both sides. Through one open shutter a forge breathes orange, and a man with forearms like hams is drawing out a bar. Pell keeps to the left-hand wall, where a run of eaves throws a strip of shade. Bram has said he's for the Song, and Sefa has turned him down on the loan, so the chain mail comes up the cobbles behind Pell. It stays well back in the alley's throat, the way Pell asked, with the box held against Bram's chest and the green seal bare to the sky. Sefa is still at the trough. The left-hand track runs off behind the yards beside her and nobody is walking it.

Pell stops a pace short of the alley mouth with the smithy's corner post at his shoulder, and looks out at the high street before the high street can look at him.

It's market morning in a smiths' town. A cart of pig iron is grinding along with one bad wheel. Two women are haggling over a crate of hens. A boy is selling hot chestnuts from a brazier on a pole. Two Flaming Fist men in faded red tabards stroll past in the middle of the street, talking about somebody's sister, and don't look at the alley. Some way along on the right a painted sign creaks on its iron bracket: a grinning man in motley with three red balls in the air. The Jovial Juggler's door stands open, and nobody is in it. Pell sees no brown coat anywhere he looks, and no lean, tall man taking his time.

The Song of the Morning stands across the street and a little to the left, behind a low wall of honey-coloured stone with the gilded sunburst high on its tower. The east door is in the side of the temple facing him, up three shallow steps under a little porch. A woman in a plain grey dress sits on the stone bench under the porch with her hands folded in her lap and a covered basket at her feet. She watches the street the way you watch for one particular person. She doesn't look old.

The smoke comes from behind the temple's wall, in a side yard Pell can just see into past the porch. A lay brother in a yellow-dyed apron is raking a heap of old rushes, wilted altar flowers and broom sweepings onto a smouldering pile. He coughs, and rakes again. The wind brings a thin line of it over the street, smelling of cedar and damp straw. Someone in the temple is burning the week's sweepings, and that's all it is.

Behind Pell the forge breathes, and the hammer comes down on the bar.

Pell hears all of it. A carter's widow, a train lost on the road to Nashkel, a forty-gold note waiting in a moneylender's box. Set beside the one line on the burnt paper in his tool roll, it fits with nothing sticking out. He turns his back to the trough, puts his shoulder into the bulk of Bram's mail so the farrier's boy sees only two backs, and counts sixteen gold pieces off the top of his purse into Bram's hand one at a time. Afterwards his purse is lighter by more than half.

Then he takes the right fork.

The alley climbs between two smithies on cobbles worn into shallow dishes. It's hot on both sides. Through one open shutter a forge breathes orange, and a man with forearms like hams is drawing out a bar. Pell keeps to the left-hand wall, where a run of eaves throws a strip of shade. Bram has said he's for the Song, and Sefa has turned him down on the loan, so the chain mail comes up the cobbles behind Pell. It stays well back in the alley's throat, the way Pell asked, with the box held against Bram's chest and the green seal bare to the sky. Sefa is still at the trough. The left-hand track runs off behind the yards beside her and nobody is walking it.

Pell stops a pace short of the alley mouth with the smithy's corner post at his shoulder, and looks out at the high street before the high street can look at him.

It's market morning in a smiths' town. A cart of pig iron is grinding along with one bad wheel. Two women are haggling over a crate of hens. A boy is selling hot chestnuts from a brazier on a pole. Two Flaming Fist men in faded red tabards stroll past in the middle of the street, talking about somebody's sister, and don't look at the alley. Some way along on the right a painted sign creaks on its iron bracket: a grinning man in motley with three red balls in the air. The Jovial Juggler's door stands open, and nobody is in it. Pell sees no brown coat anywhere he looks, and no lean, tall man taking his time.

The Song of the Morning stands across the street and a little to the left, behind a low wall of honey-coloured stone with the gilded sunburst high on its tower. The east door is in the side of the temple facing him, up three shallow steps under a little porch. A woman in a plain grey dress sits on the stone bench under the porch with her hands folded in her lap and a covered basket at her feet. She watches the street the way you watch for one particular person. She doesn't look old.

The smoke comes from behind the temple's wall, in a side yard Pell can just see into past the porch. A lay brother in a yellow-dyed apron is raking a heap of old rushes, wilted altar flowers and broom sweepings onto a smouldering pile. He coughs, and rakes again. The wind brings a thin line of it over the street, smelling of cedar and damp straw. Someone in the temple is burning the week's sweepings, and that's all it is.

Behind Pell the forge breathes, and the hammer comes down on the bar.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell watches the two Fist men until they're well past the alley mouth, then steps back into the shade and turns to Bram, keeping his voice under the hammer.

"It's clear. The smoke's only a brother burning sweepings. Two Fist in tabards just walked by, and there's no brown coat." He nods across the street. "Woman in grey on the bench at the east porch, basket at her feet, watching for someone. Is that Odda?"

He reaches over and folds a flap of the blanket loosely across the lid, so the green doesn't show to the street but nothing presses on the wax. "There. Bedding. If the Fist see a strange seal, they'll ask questions, and we've no good answers yet."

Then he looks past Bram, down the alley to the trough where Sefa is still standing. He doesn't shout. He catches her eye, taps two fingers to his chest and points up the alley: *with us*. Then he holds up a palm: *a few minutes*. If she comes, good. If she won't, at least she knows where they are.

"Here's what I'll do," he says to Bram. "You see to Odda. That's your business and your coin, and I won't stand over you while you do it. Keep the box on your arm and don't set it down. I'll go in the east door and find whoever's keeping Jassan. I'll ask when they bury him, and whether the cord's still round his neck." A beat. "If anything happens while I'm inside, a brown coat, anyone reaching for that bundle, you shout, and I'll be out before you've finished."

He waits for a gap behind the pig-iron cart and crosses at an unhurried walk, as if he has prayers to say. Passing the woman on the bench, he gives her a small polite nod and a good look: her face, her hands, the basket, and whether she's waiting for Bram or for someone else entirely. Then he climbs the three steps and goes in under the porch.

Inside, he stops a pace past the door to let his eyes adjust and finds the nearest priest or lay brother.

"Morning, brother. I'm here for Jassan Ferr, the clerk from the Coast Way. Your people brought him in three days back. When does he go in the ground? And I need to ask after something small he wore."

Out of game: I'd like an Insight read on the woman as I pass, and a Perception check on the street and the temple interior for Brannock or anyone watching. Inside I'm looking for whoever has charge of the dead.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Thank you, Pell. Sixteen back from my fee today.”

I stop when I realise I’ve followed him toward the temple. “I’m taking the box to Vell’s, then. Ask Odda to wait for us, if you find her.”

I turn back to the trough and take the left-hand track with Sefa, keeping the box level.

“I have the forty now,” I tell her quietly. “I’ll ask to purchase Harl Brand’s note. No need to mention Odda. Once that’s settled, we deliver the box and collect our pay.”

scenes.narration:
Pell watches the two red tabards until they're three stalls past the alley mouth and arguing with the chestnut boy about the price. Then he steps back into the strip of shade. He tells Bram what he saw in a few words under the hammer, reaches across and lays one loose flap of the blanket over the lid. The wool settles over the green without touching the wax. From the street the box now looks like a bundle of bedding a man is carrying home.

He looks back down the alley to the trough at the bottom, taps two fingers to his chest, points up the cobbles, then holds up a flat palm. He doesn't call out, and the forge noise would drown him if he did.

Bram hears out the plan: Odda for Bram, the east door for Pell, *shout if anything happens*. He thanks Pell for the sixteen and says it comes back out of his fee today. Then he stops, and you can see him notice he's halfway up an alley he didn't mean to climb. He's taking the box to Vell's, he says, and if Pell finds Odda, he can ask her to wait for them. He turns round with the bundle held level and goes back down the cobbles toward the trough and the left-hand track. The forge breathes orange as his mail passes the open shutter, and then the alley swallows him.

Pell waits for the pig-iron cart to grind past on its bad wheel and crosses behind it at the pace of a man who has prayers to say and is in no hurry about them. His route takes him along the low honey-coloured wall and past the porch steps.

He nods to the woman on the bench, and as he does he looks at her properly.

He reads her without trying. She's younger than the grey makes her look, thirty perhaps, with a carter's wife's hands: red knuckles, a burn scar across the back of one thumb, a thin brass ring she keeps turning with her other thumb and doesn't seem to know she's turning. Her eyes come to him when he steps out of the alley mouth, and the way they come is a question. Then she sees no mail and no shield, and her face closes. Her eyes slide past him and stay on the alley's shadowed throat. She isn't counting the street or signalling anyone, and she's watching nobody else. She's waiting for one man, she's afraid he won't come, and she's been afraid of it since early morning. The covered basket at her feet hasn't been touched. When he nods she gives him a quick nod back, the kind you give a stranger, and goes on watching the alley he came out of.

Pell takes the three shallow steps and goes in under the porch.

Inside, the Song of the Morning is cool and smells of beeswax and old stone. He stops a pace past the door to let his eyes catch up. Tall east windows of pale yellow glass turn the flat white morning gold. It's quiet. Two old women kneel near the front with their beads, and at the far end a lay brother on a ladder is trimming candles. Nearer, at a side door with a curtain of undyed linen, a heavyset priest of fifty or so sits on a stool with a ledger open on his knee. His robe is rose-coloured and faded nearly to cream at the cuffs, and his sleeves are rolled like a man who'd sooner be lifting something. He looks up at the sound of boots.

Pell asks his questions.

The priest closes the ledger on his thumb and takes his time looking at him, the way a man looks at someone who has come about the dead.

"Brother Aldane. And yes, he's ours." He tips his head toward the linen curtain. "He's through there, in the cold room. We put him in the ground at first light tomorrow. Lathander's hour. No kin came forward, so it'll be the brothers and me, and whoever else wants to stand there." He thinks about the second question before answering it. "Something small he wore. You mean the cord." It isn't a question. "It's on him. We wash them, we dress them, and we bury them with what they came in wearing, unless someone with a right to it asks." He looks at Pell's hands, at the satchel, at the shortsword on the right hip, and then back at his face, not unkindly. "You'd be from Ostrin Vell, I expect. His boy was here yesterday asking the same thing, and I told him what I'll tell you, friend. Master Vell is welcome to come himself and say what's his."

He lets the ledger fall open again on his knee, but he doesn't look down at it.

"You're the second to ask after the key." A short pause. "You're the first to ask when we bury him."

Behind him the linen curtain stirs a little in a draught from the cold room, and Pell catches the faint, clean smell of lime. At the far end the lay brother pinches out a candle, and the two old women go on with their beads.

What the players wrote for this round, in the round's order (each paragraph is that character's):
<<<
Pell Dunmore: Pell watches the two Fist men until they're well past the alley mouth, then steps back into the shade and turns to Bram, keeping his voice under the hammer.

"It's clear. The smoke's only a brother burning sweepings. Two Fist in tabards just walked by, and there's no brown coat." He nods across the street. "Woman in grey on the bench at the east porch, basket at her feet, watching for someone. Is that Odda?"

He reaches over and folds a flap of the blanket loosely across the lid, so the green doesn't show to the street but nothing presses on the wax. "There. Bedding. If the Fist see a strange seal, they'll ask questions, and we've no good answers yet."

Then he looks past Bram, down the alley to the trough where Sefa is still standing. He doesn't shout. He catches her eye, taps two fingers to his chest and points up the alley: *with us*. Then he holds up a palm: *a few minutes*. If she comes, good. If she won't, at least she knows where they are.

"Here's what I'll do," he says to Bram. "You see to Odda. That's your business and your coin, and I won't stand over you while you do it. Keep the box on your arm and don't set it down. I'll go in the east door and find whoever's keeping Jassan. I'll ask when they bury him, and whether the cord's still round his neck." A beat. "If anything happens while I'm inside, a brown coat, anyone reaching for that bundle, you shout, and I'll be out before you've finished."

He waits for a gap behind the pig-iron cart and crosses at an unhurried walk, as if he has prayers to say. Passing the woman on the bench, he gives her a small polite nod and a good look: her face, her hands, the basket, and whether she's waiting for Bram or for someone else entirely. Then he climbs the three steps and goes in under the porch.

Inside, he stops a pace past the door to let his eyes adjust and finds the nearest priest or lay brother.

"Morning, brother. I'm here for Jassan Ferr, the clerk from the Coast Way. Your people brought him in three days back. When does he go in the ground? And I need to ask after something small he wore."

Out of game: I'd like an Insight read on the woman as I pass, and a Perception check on the street and the temple interior for Brannock or anyone watching. Inside I'm looking for whoever has charge of the dead.

Bram Halloway: “Thank you, Pell. Sixteen back from my fee today.”

I stop when I realise I’ve followed him toward the temple. “I’m taking the box to Vell’s, then. Ask Odda to wait for us, if you find her.”

I turn back to the trough and take the left-hand track with Sefa, keeping the box level.

“I have the forty now,” I tell her quietly. “I’ll ask to purchase Harl Brand’s note. No need to mention Odda. Once that’s settled, we deliver the box and collect our pay.”
>>>

Your narration:
<<<
Pell watches the two red tabards until they're three stalls past the alley mouth and arguing with the chestnut boy about the price. Then he steps back into the strip of shade. He tells Bram what he saw in a few words under the hammer, reaches across and lays one loose flap of the blanket over the lid. The wool settles over the green without touching the wax. From the street the box now looks like a bundle of bedding a man is carrying home.

He looks back down the alley to the trough at the bottom, taps two fingers to his chest, points up the cobbles, then holds up a flat palm. He doesn't call out, and the forge noise would drown him if he did.

Bram hears out the plan: Odda for Bram, the east door for Pell, *shout if anything happens*. He thanks Pell for the sixteen and says it comes back out of his fee today. Then he stops, and you can see him notice he's halfway up an alley he didn't mean to climb. He's taking the box to Vell's, he says, and if Pell finds Odda, he can ask her to wait for them. He turns round with the bundle held level and goes back down the cobbles toward the trough and the left-hand track. The forge breathes orange as his mail passes the open shutter, and then the alley swallows him.

Pell waits for the pig-iron cart to grind past on its bad wheel and crosses behind it at the pace of a man who has prayers to say and is in no hurry about them. His route takes him along the low honey-coloured wall and past the porch steps.

He nods to the woman on the bench, and as he does he looks at her properly.

He reads her without trying. She's younger than the grey makes her look, thirty perhaps, with a carter's wife's hands: red knuckles, a burn scar across the back of one thumb, a thin brass ring she keeps turning with her other thumb and doesn't seem to know she's turning. Her eyes come to him when he steps out of the alley mouth, and the way they come is a question. Then she sees no mail and no shield, and her face closes. Her eyes slide past him and stay on the alley's shadowed throat. She isn't counting the street or signalling anyone, and she's watching nobody else. She's waiting for one man, she's afraid he won't come, and she's been afraid of it since early morning. The covered basket at her feet hasn't been touched. When he nods she gives him a quick nod back, the kind you give a stranger, and goes on watching the alley he came out of.

Pell takes the three shallow steps and goes in under the porch.

Inside, the Song of the Morning is cool and smells of beeswax and old stone. He stops a pace past the door to let his eyes catch up. Tall east windows of pale yellow glass turn the flat white morning gold. It's quiet. Two old women kneel near the front with their beads, and at the far end a lay brother on a ladder is trimming candles. Nearer, at a side door with a curtain of undyed linen, a heavyset priest of fifty or so sits on a stool with a ledger open on his knee. His robe is rose-coloured and faded nearly to cream at the cuffs, and his sleeves are rolled like a man who'd sooner be lifting something. He looks up at the sound of boots.

Pell asks his questions.

The priest closes the ledger on his thumb and takes his time looking at him, the way a man looks at someone who has come about the dead.

"Brother Aldane. And yes, he's ours." He tips his head toward the linen curtain. "He's through there, in the cold room. We put him in the ground at first light tomorrow. Lathander's hour. No kin came forward, so it'll be the brothers and me, and whoever else wants to stand there." He thinks about the second question before answering it. "Something small he wore. You mean the cord." It isn't a question. "It's on him. We wash them, we dress them, and we bury them with what they came in wearing, unless someone with a right to it asks." He looks at Pell's hands, at the satchel, at the shortsword on the right hip, and then back at his face, not unkindly. "You'd be from Ostrin Vell, I expect. His boy was here yesterday asking the same thing, and I told him what I'll tell you, friend. Master Vell is welcome to come himself and say what's his."

He lets the ledger fall open again on his knee, but he doesn't look down at it.

"You're the second to ask after the key." A short pause. "You're the first to ask when we bury him."

Behind him the linen curtain stirs a little in a draught from the cold room, and Pell catches the faint, clean smell of lime. At the far end the lay brother pinches out a candle, and the two old women go on with their beads.
>>>

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa watches Bram out of sight, one hand resting on the trough's stone lip. The farrier's boy has stopped staring and gone back to his buckets, sloshing water with more care than before.

She takes a breath, then follows the right fork at a slower pace than Pell, keeping to the shade and the wall. The alley's throat is loud with hammer strikes and the clink of hot iron going into the slack-tub. At the corner she stops just behind Pell, close enough to murmur against the noise.

"I'll shadow the street from here a moment. See if anyone's watching the Song's east door — or watching you."

cards.title: Perception (Wisdom +0): is anyone watching the Song's east door, or Pell?

presses.text:
Sefa stands at the corner with her back to the smithy post, her head turning slowly as if watching traffic, the way a woman waiting on someone does. Her eyes move along the street and across the front of the Song of the Morning.

Pell has gone in cleanly enough, and no one in the street has broken stride to follow him — no loiterer straightening off a wall, no trader suddenly forgetting his cart, no second man moving when the first doesn't. The grey woman on the bench takes no more notice of her than before. But she knows better than to trust a still picture. A watcher doesn't have to move to be a watcher.

She doesn't cross the street yet. She stays in the shade of the alley, within sight of the porch and the bench, and lets the minutes run while the smithies hammer behind her. If Brannock or one of Thale's people is marking the temple, he'll show himself the moment Pell comes back out with news — or the moment he doesn't.
presses.reply:
Got it. I'll take that paragraph as how Sefa is watching: back to the smithy post, head turning as if she's watching traffic, staying in the alley's shade within sight of the porch and the bench, not crossing yet, and waiting to see who moves when Pell comes out, or doesn't.

The parts about what she sees are the die's to decide, not mine or yours. That covers whether anyone in the street broke stride, whether there's a still watcher, and how the woman on the bench reacts to her. The card for Sefa's Perception (Wisdom +0, DC 15) still stands as called, because spotting a watcher who doesn't want to be seen is genuinely uncertain. Press Onward, or use one of your rerolls if you want to, and I'll tell you what she actually notices, written the way you've set her up.

presses.text:
You stay where you are, back to the corner post, watching the street in slow turns. The smithies hammer on either side, and the high street goes about its business: a handcart with a wobbling wheel, two old men outside the farrier's sharing a pipe, a girl with a tray of buns calling by the corner. A priest in a pale linen stole comes down the outer stair of the Song, steps over a boy at the bottom and turns west, not east. The woman in grey sits with her hands motionless in her lap, her eyes level with yours for a second, then away. Her face gives nothing but endurance. She could be any widow waiting on business; she could be watching.

No one breaks stride. No one straightens off a wall or leaves in the wake of Pell going in or you coming up. But the street is moving enough that a man could stand where the wall is in shadow and never have to move at all.

The bell has not rung eleven. The grey woman hasn't gone in.

Where you are: the alley mouth, with the sun onto your back from the forge-smoke behind · Time: Day 1 · late morning

Round 16 — what does Sefa Marrin do?
presses.reply: Got it. As before, I'll take this as how Sefa is watching. She keeps her back to the corner post at the alley mouth, turns her head slowly the way someone watching traffic does, stays put and doesn't cross toward the porch or the bench yet. The rest of the paragraph describes what she sees: the passers-by, a priest on the outer stair, whether anyone moves after Pell, what the woman in grey does when their eyes meet. That part is the die's and mine to settle, so I'll set it aside rather than make it fact. Her Perception card (Wisdom +0, DC 15) still stands, because spotting someone who stands still in shadow and doesn't want to be seen is genuinely uncertain. Press Onward, or spend one of your rerolls if you want to, and I'll tell you what she actually notices from that post. One small thing: the 'Round 16' line and the 'late morning' at the end look like the app's prompt pasted in. The clock still reads mid-morning, a little past ten, and the bell hasn't rung eleven.

presses.text:
I'll set the street aside, then, and stop reading what isn't mine to know. What Sefa saw, her eyes alone will tell her — and the card says her eyes told her nothing simple.

I keep to the shade and let my gaze move like a woman counting windows. There is no second glance from the grey woman. She holds still, hands in her lap, as if I'd been a thought that crossed the yard and left again. The smithies keep their hammering, and the street between the pillars is full of ordinary feet.

Pell is inside. Bram by now is along the left track with the box, and I am the one who stayed. For the moment I stay — within sight of the east door, out of the daylight, waiting on a sign that will not come because someone knows how not to move.
presses.reply:
Got it. I'll take this as Sefa's action: she stays in the shade at the alley mouth, within sight of the east door, watching the street like a woman counting windows, and doesn't cross yet.

The rest of your paragraph is a proposal, and I'll settle it when you press Onward. That covers how the woman in grey does or doesn't react, what the street holds, and whether anyone out there "knows how not to move." One thing to keep in mind: a check that doesn't go her way only means Sefa can't tell from where she stands. It doesn't mean someone is there. I'll narrate what her eyes actually give her, and no more.

One point on where people are. Bram's player declared that he takes the left-hand track to Vell's "with Sefa." Your paragraphs have Sefa at the alley mouth, so Bram goes on with the box and Sefa stays where you've put her, unless you tell me otherwise.

The card is still waiting. Press Onward, or spend one of your rerolls if you'd like.

presses.text:
You stay in the shade at the alley mouth, and Bram disappears along the left track with the box and no clear agreement about who goes with him. The smithy's heat rolls in waves across the cobbles, and the shadows of the high street have shortened to noonside. You watch the grey woman. She does not look at you again.

The street keeps its ordinary face. A shutter bangs open somewhere above; the bun girl's cry comes up the street and turns another corner; the two old men with the pipe finish and go their ways, one east past the Song, one west. A carter rumbles down from the high street and stops at the farrier's. For a long count, nobody comes out of the east door after Pell, and nobody goes in. A boy with a broom steps out onto the porch steps, sweeps the dust in a half-moon about the posts, and goes back in. The watcher, if there is one, is too still to see.

The air is warm with iron and bread-smoke now, and the smell of the forge is in the wool of your clothes. The grey woman shifts her basket with one foot, out of the path of a cart wheel splashing muddy water. The cart rolls past without touching her, and she settles back. Her eyes have gone past the alley again, patient as the dead.

High over the roofs, the smoke of the Song's kitchen or incense climbs thin into the dull noon. Around the temple's stonework, no pigeons start. The street gives you no one.

[You have no other pending rolls. The bell still has not rung for eleven.]

opening.narration:
Beregost wakes to hammers. From every smithy along the street the ringing comes through the shutters of Ostrin Vell's counting-house, where the morning light falls on brass scales and rows of bound ledgers. Sefa Marrin, Pell Dunmore and Bram Halloway stand at the long counter. The three of you met here only this morning, and Vell has just hired you together.

Vell lays the terms out a second time, tapping the counter with one finger at each point. Jassan Ferr, his clerk, died three days ago in a rented room above the cooper's yard on the Coast Way. In that room is a locked strongbox of ledgers. Vell wants it here before nightfall today, unopened, with its seal whole. On delivery he will pay seventy-five gold for the three of you to share. Not a copper before.

Beside the counter stands a clerk's desk. Its stool is pushed neatly under it, the inkwell is capped and the blotter is clean, as if someone had tidied it and no one had sat there since. Vell does not look at it. He looks from Sefa to Pell to Bram, folds his hands on the counter and waits. "The Coast Way is not far, and the day will not wait for you. Is there anything you need to ask me before you go?"

screens.text:
The session begins.

Beregost wakes to hammers. From every smithy along the street the ringing comes through the shutters of Ostrin Vell's counting-house, where morning light falls on brass scales and rows of bound ledgers. You stand at the long counter with Sefa Marrin and Pell Dunmore. You met them only this morning, and Vell has just hired the three of you together.

Vell lays out the terms a second time, tapping the counter with one finger at each point. Jassan Ferr, his clerk, died three days ago in a rented room above the cooper's yard on the Coast Way. In that room is a locked strongbox of ledgers. Vell wants it here before nightfall today, unopened, with its seal whole. On delivery he will pay seventy-five gold for the three of you to share. Not a copper before.

Beside the counter stands a clerk's desk. Its stool is pushed neatly under it, the inkwell is capped and the blotter is clean, as if someone had tidied it and no one had sat there since. Vell does not look at it. He looks from Sefa to Pell to you, folds his hands on the counter and waits. "The Coast Way is not far, and the day will not wait for you. Is there anything you need to ask me before you go?"

Your records:
Bram Halloway — Human, fighter 5 (Champion; Protection fighting style), former caravan guard of the Trade Way, level 5
HP 44/44 · AC 18 · Speed 30 feet
STR 17 · DEX 12 · CON 15 · INT 10 · WIS 13 · CHA 10
Skills: Athletics +6; Perception +4; Survival +4; Intimidation +3; Tools: land vehicles +3
Saves: Strength saving throw +6 (proficient); Constitution saving throw +5 (proficient); Dexterity saving throw +1; Intelligence saving throw +0; Wisdom saving throw +1; Charisma saving throw +0
Attacks: Longsword +6 to hit, 1d8+3 slashing (1d10+3 two-handed); Javelin +6 to hit, 1d6+3 piercing, range 30/120; Extra Attack: two attacks with the Attack action
Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Extra Attack: attacks twice when taking the Attack action; Fighting style, Protection: with a shield, a reaction imposes disadvantage on an attack against a creature within 5 feet of him; Second Wind: a bonus action, regains 1d10+5 hit points; once per short rest; Action Surge: one additional action on his turn; once per short rest; Improved Critical (Champion): a weapon attack crits on 19 or 20; Healer's kit: stabilises a dying creature without a check (ten uses)
Limits: No magic at all; Heavy armour: disadvantage on Stealth; Second Wind and Action Surge return only after a short rest
Counters: Hit dice 5/5; Second wind 1/1; Action surge 1/1; Heroic inspiration 0/1
Money: 23 gp; 14 sp; 30 cp
Worn: Armor / clothing: Chain Mail; Main hand: Longsword; Off hand: Shield
Pack: Bedroll and Hardtack; Healer's Kit; Hempen Rope (50 feet); Javelin ×4; Tinderbox; Torch ×3

Where you are: Ostrin Vell's counting-house, Beregost · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 1 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Sefa stands with her hands folded on the counter, prayer beads wound around one wrist, and gives Vell a steady, patient look. She asks what the clerk died of and who found him. Then she asks whether anyone was sent for the strongbox before you: a landlord with another key, a relative who came searching, or some other man working for Vell. She says she would rather know whether the door will be locked, or standing open with someone waiting behind it.

Pell leans an elbow on the counter, his eyes going first to the empty desk and then back to Vell. He asks how Jassan died, who holds the key now, and who else knows about the box. He also asks what the seal looks like, so that nobody can later say you broke it. He keeps his eyes on Vell throughout.

Ostrin Vell takes the questions the way he takes coin: one at a time, and slowly.

"His heart," he says to Sefa first. "Wenna Pike found him. She keeps the house over the cooper's yard. She went up for the rent on the morning after and he was in his chair at the table, cold. A man from the Fist came, looked at him and wrote it down. Heart. Jassan was forty-one." His finger stops on the counter. "Hearts stop."

He turns to you and Pell together, since you asked the same thing. "Nobody watches it. It is behind Wenna's lock. She has the key, and she has Jassan's rent owing, she tells me. I sent my boy for the box the day before yesterday. She sent him back. Nothing leaves that room, she says, until someone pays what he owed her." His mouth thins. "The box is mine. The rent was his."

"Who else knows?" Vell repeats. "My house. Wenna Pike. Anyone Wenna has talked to in three days, and she talks." A small pause. "He had no family here. His mother was in the Gate, and she has been dead for years."

For the seal, Vell opens a drawer under the counter and takes out a brass seal matrix on a short wooden handle. He warms a stub of brown wax at the lamp, lets a drop fall on a scrap of paper and presses the matrix into it. When he lifts it, the mark is a ring with a V inside it and a small flaw at the top of the ring, where the brass once cracked.

"Brown wax. That mark. Jassan sealed for the house. Every box." He pushes the scrap across the counter so it lies between the three of you. "If it is not whole, I will know it."

Then he dips a pen and writes without stopping to think, in a small upright hand: *The bearers collect the strongbox of Jassan Ferr on behalf of the house of Ostrin Vell. Beregost.* He signs it, sands it, shakes it off and lays it on the counter in front of you, next to the wax impression.

"The key is Wenna's. I have none." He puts the brass matrix back in its drawer and locks it. "The rent is between her and you, if you choose to pay it. I will not."

Outside, the hammers along the street have found a rhythm. The light in the window has moved a hand's width across the scales. Vell takes the nearest ledger, opens it, and doesn't look at the clerk's desk.

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: Vell's strongbox
+ Quest: Vell's strongbox

Where you are: Ostrin Vell's moneylending shop, at the counter · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 2 — what does Bram Halloway do?

You leave the letter on the counter and put it to Vell: he sent a boy, she refused him, and now he pays three armed strangers to try again. You ask how much rent is owing, and say you won't draw steel on a landlady over a tenant's debts. You ask whether he will deduct what you pay her from Ferr's estate and reimburse you against a receipt, up to a sum agreed now, or else your fee is whatever is left.

Beside you, Pell had already lifted the wax scrap off the counter and turned it to the window light, running a thumbnail along it. He said that setting one mark beside the other beats trying to recall it later, and tucked the scrap into an inner pocket. He then asked Vell how much Wenna said was owed, who the boy was and whether he got past her door, whether anyone had been in the room since, whether Jassan carried a key, papers or a ring, and whether the Fist man took anything. Vell doesn't reach for the scrap.

"Keep it. It is wax." He closes his ledger on one finger to hold the page.

"Three gold and some silver. That is what she told the boy." He taps the ledger once for each answer. "The boy is Mott. He did not get past her door. She met him on the stairs with her arms folded, he says, and he came down again. If anyone has been in since, Wenna will know. It is her house."

He goes on. "Jassan kept the box key on a cord round his neck. The Song of the Morning took him for burial. Whether the key went with him, ask them. The Fist man I never saw. He came to the house, not here. He wrote it in their book at the garrison. Whatever he took, he did not bring to me."

Your question gets a longer look than any of Pell's. Vell sits working out the sum.

"I will not pay Wenna Pike." He says it plainly. "But I owe Jassan his wages for the last tenday. Four gold. He has no heirs here to claim it." He sets the ledger down. "Bring me her receipt for the rent, signed, with the box. I will pay it to you out of his wages, on top of the seventy-five. Up to four gold. Not a copper over, and no receipt, no money." He takes up his pen. "That is his debt settled from his own pay. It is not mine."

Your letter still lies on the counter. Pell has straightened up, looking at the door, and has nodded toward it, saying they should go to the Coast Way and look over the cooper's yard before the day wears on. Sefa is still at the counter. Outside, a cart rattles past toward the Coast Way, and a smithy starts a new piece with three heavy strokes. Vell goes back to writing figures in his small, upright hand.

Where you are: Vell's counting-room, by the counter · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 3 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Vell doesn't argue. He writes a line beneath his signature on the bearer's note: up to four gold of J. Ferr's owed wages, against W. Pike's signed receipt for his rent, paid with the fee on delivery of the box, seal whole. He signs it a second time, sands it and pushes the paper back. Pell snatches it up first and blows the sand off, while Sefa has a hand on the other corner. Between the two of them it is folded once along its crease and ends up in your hand. Vell tells Sefa "Before nightfall," and gives Pell a short, level nod. He has the ledger open again before the door shuts behind you.

Outside, you say you want to talk to Wenna before spending anything, since she found Ferr and may know more than that his heart stopped. Sefa agrees, saying three gold and some silver is cheaper than a fight in a stairwell, and that you should see what Wenna Pike actually wants. Pell says he doesn't like the key on Ferr's neck or a Fist man nobody has seen, and that someone may have had the box open and closed again. He offers to pay Wenna from his own purse if need be, recovering it through the receipt, and says that while you and Sefa speak with her, he'll look over the stairs, the door and the lock. If the box key isn't in that room, the Song of the Morning is where he wants to go afterwards. Then he heads off toward the Coast Way, eyes on the rooflines.

Beregost runs on charcoal and iron. Smoke hangs low over the roofs, and hammering comes from three directions, never quite together. The Coast Way runs west off the high street past a farrier's, a chandler's and two houses with washing out. It is a quarter of an hour's walk, and carts make you step aside twice.

You hear the cooper's yard before you see it: someone driving hoops onto a barrel with a mallet, slow and steady, stopping every few strokes to check the fit. The house sits over the yard and comes right up to the street, two storeys of timber on a stone footing with a plastered front gone yellow. The ground-floor window is open, with a curtain and a pot of something green on the sill. A woman's voice inside is scolding someone about the state of the step. The two front windows upstairs have their shutters open. Pell stays across the lane looking the house over while you and Sefa head for the gate.

Behind the gate the mallet stops. A broad, bald man in a leather apron looks round the end of a row of barrels, sees a man in chain mail with a shield and a paper in his hand at the gate, and comes no closer. He calls over his shoulder toward the house, not loudly: "Wenna. More of them."

The voice at the ground-floor window stops in the middle of what it was saying.

(While the others were looking elsewhere, a boy pressed a sealed letter into your hand and was gone before anyone else saw. It is for you alone. You break the seal and read:)

«Bram — Harl died owing Ostrin Vell forty gold. Vell's note for it is in his dead clerk's strongbox with the rest; Jassan wrote to me before he died that it will be called on the house the day after the box goes back. Vell's counting-house sells such a note back for its face to whoever pays it at the counter before it is entered in his books. If you can, pay the forty gold for it before nightfall, before the box is opened, and the house stays ours. I have nothing left to give. — Odda Brand»

Your records, changed:
Carried: + Vell's Note to the Bearers

Your journal, new:
+ Promise: Vell's written offer: Jassan's wages for the rent

Where you are: at the gate of the cooper's yard, Coast Way · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 4 — what does Bram Halloway do?

You read the letter twice, fold it into your coat, and stand still a moment with your jaw tight. Then you turn back to the gate, keeping Vell's paper low. You give your name, say you've come about Jassan Ferr's strongbox and to settle the rent against a signed receipt, and add that there's no need for trouble. You stay outside the gate and say Vell's boy should have come prepared to pay.

Sefa had stayed a half-step behind you and to one side, her hands in plain view of the cooper, and had not touched the gate. She called mildly toward the house for Mistress Pike. She said you'd come about Jassan Ferr's room, that you'd rather talk to her than tramp up her stair like the last one, and that you'd mind the step.

Pell crossed the lane at an easy pace, crouched by the gatepost as if for a loose bootlace, and straightened. He stepped up behind you and Sefa and said quietly that you shouldn't look down. He said there is Guild chalk from the Gate on the left gatepost at knee height, a day or two old, a mark meaning the place is claimed, watched, and to be avoided. As Beregost has no Guild, he said, someone must have carried it in. He also noted that the cooper said "more of them", so you aren't the first today. Then he asked the cooper aloud, in a friendly way, who the others were, and drifted half a step aside to watch the lane. He left the mark as it was.

The ground-floor curtain twitches. The street door opens and a short, broad-hipped woman past fifty comes out onto the step, sleeves pushed up, a rag in her fist and a ring of three keys on a cord at her apron. She looks at the step first, then at the three of you.

"Well, somebody was raised right," she says to Sefa. "*Mind the step.* That boy of Vell's came up it like a goat. Tobin, it's all right, they're not the other one." The cooper doesn't go back to his mallet just yet.

She watches you, then hears you out, and her arms come up and fold across her chest. She doesn't look like she's refusing anyone. She looks like she's settling in for a long talk.

You ask Sefa for the sixteen, and tell Pell to go after the key if he thinks time is short. Sefa answers you both in her sickbed-door voice. The box goes left to Vell's, her share isn't hers to lend until the seal is on his counter, and nobody says Odda's name to Vell.

Pell turns his back to the trough, puts his shoulder into the bulk of your mail so the farrier's boy sees only two backs, and counts sixteen gold pieces into your hand one at a time.

Then he takes the right fork. The alley climbs between two smithies on cobbles worn into shallow dishes. It's hot on both sides. Through one open shutter a forge breathes orange, and a man with forearms like hams is drawing out a bar. Pell keeps to the left-hand wall in the strip of shade from the eaves. You follow well back in the alley's throat, the box held against your chest and the green seal bare to the sky. Sefa is still at the trough. The left-hand track runs off behind the yards beside her and nobody is walking it.

Pell stops a pace short of the alley mouth, at a smithy's corner post, looking out at the high street. Behind him the forge breathes, and the hammer comes down on the bar.
